speakeroldname: Mr. PIUS MICHAUD (Restigouche and Madawaska) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable for the purpose of the preservation of our great forest wealth that the government of Canada should co-operate with the governments of the several provinces.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I have taken a
special interest in the Canadian Forestry Association for many years, and have also read carefully all forestry reports published by that asociation and by the Forestry branch of the Department of Interior. I beg to congratulate and to thank the personnel of these two bodies for their splendid work. They have taken great pains to secure information on this important subject and I am more than thankful to them for the facts which I have been enabled to obtain in connection therewith. We are told that a country without a forest is like a man without a heart. We have forests in this country, the estimated value of which is over two billion dollars, an amount sufficient to pay our present national debt. In 1922, there were over 4,000 forest fires in Canada, and Mr. Robson Black, secretary of the Canadian Forestry Association, has stated that these fires destroyed more lumber than all our forest industries or our own lumbermen could consume in many years of operation. Further, he states that the timber limits destroyed last year would cover a space between Halifax and Winnipeg a mile in width. I have here a report published in one of the Ottawa newspapers of a meeting held

Forest Protection
recently in this city. At this meeting Mr. W. H. Shapley, who presided, made some remarks in connection with our forest industries. He is reported thus:
Time and money was spent to prevent disease and loss	in agriculture,	laws were	enacted	to	prevent
workingmen being injured, and capable men were doing research work in many departments, but little or no attention was paid to means of preventing fire loss.
Mr. Shapley stated that the annual fire loss in the Dominion was a disgrace to its citizens. Complaints were	being made of	the burden	of taxation,	yet fewwere	disturbed over	an annual	fire loss	of	45 millions and many valuable lives.Responsibility for	conditions	as they	were could
not be placed upon the fire fighting organizations maintained in this country. The fundamental error was that too great stress was placed on the extinguishing of fires and too little emphasis placed on the necessity of safeguarding the hazards from which fire originate.
There is not a province in the Dominion which has not its timber limits and I know that the government of each province desires the heartiest co-operation in order to preserve its natural wealth. I was very much interested in an article published recently on this subject, in its bearing on the province of New Brunswick. I would quote the following:
The annual agricultural and forest crops of New Brunswick comprise about 85 per cent of the total value of all products produced. The forests cover about 70 per cent of the total area of the province, and the total value of the forest products produced averages about $35,000,000. Agricultural products in 1922 were valued at $42,965,000. These two great industries, lumbering and farming, combine to keep
New Brunswick stable	There are thirtyfour acres of forest land for every man, woman and child in the province, while cultivated farming land under field crops aggregates two and one-half acres per capita.
The rural population is much greater than the total in towns and cities. Farming communities in fertile valleys and on rich uplands are surrounded by forests. During the long winter months when the prairie farmer the potato planter and the fruit grower are more or less idle, the New Brunswick farmer is busily engaged cutting logs either in the timber limits of the lumber companies or on his own wood-lot getting out logs, latlnvood, pulpwood or cordwood. Did you ever meet a man from rural New Brunswick who did not know how to use an axe? It is estimated that 10,00 men are employed in the lumber woods this winter.	More than $2,000,000 will be paid out in
wages and board before the annual cut of fifteen million logs will be safely skidded on the bank of the streams.	The forest payroll of the long winter
months keeps the farm on a stable footing in that period between harvesting and sowing. If the reader doubts this statement, let him ask any of the merchants in the rural districts about conditions during the 1921-22 season when the depression in the lumber industry was at the lowest level, and there was little or no work in the woods. The same condition would arise and exist for a century if these same forest trees were burned.
The flames that destroyed many homes, wrecked business and caused the death of many men were contributed to to a greater or less extent by the carelessness of lumber men, campers and others who frequent our for-52
ests. In this connection allow me to repeat the words of a United States forestry commissioner. In a report recently submitted to Congress-which, by the way, was read at a meeting of our Forestry Association held in Ottawa-concerning the damage to American forests, it is declared:
When the iorests fail the lumber business, one of the greatest industries of the country will disappear. Suffering among all building trades will follow; mining will become vastly more expensive. The price of coal, iron and other minerals will rise. When this occurs the railways will be directly affected and the cost of transportation will increase. In brief, when forests commence to fail every man, woman, and child in the United States will feel the pinch. Through past misuse forests are undoubtedly failing.
There is a lesson for Canada here. Experts have readily admitted that Canadian forests constitute one of the world's greatest reserves of timber. That they should be ruthlessly wasted by fire and other agencies is tragic and unnecessary.
While it is true that the government has done much to protect the forests, there is very much that yet remains to be done. The population of the consuming area tributary to our forests has increased fivefold during the past half century, but its wood consumption, has increased tenfold or more. The natural resources of Canada are the envy of the world. To squander these resources is nothing less than criminal.
On reliable information it seems that about 150,000,000 cords of wood, or fifty years' supply, were destroyed by insects in the last ten years in the province of Quebec. In the same province 800,000 acres were burned over in 1921, and only a little over 1,000 acres were planted. And still millions of trees were exported from eastern Canada to the United States in the same year. The Boston Herald, in connection with this great destruction, says: What adds to the pity is that most of the timber destroyed by our woodland fires is so young as to belong to generations not old enough to protect it.
So far, I believe, the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick have the most practical laws to protect their forest reserves. I have in my possession the Forest Act of the province of New Brunswick. This was passed in 1918 and has been amended from time to time since. I must admit that in New Brunswick we have copied to a certain extent legislation enacted by the province of Quebec. Let me acknowledge, Mr. Speaker, that the province of Quebec with its great forest reserves has given an excellent example to all the other provinces of how to take care of this natural Wealth.
Reports, based on comprehensive surveys, have been published by the Commission of

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this is a subject which has not sufficiently impressed the people of the country generally; there are only a few men in Canada who realize its importance. We have one man in the Maritime provinces who is so strongly impressed with the necessity of protecting our forests that he is spending a large amount of money in a personal campaign to educate the public in this connection. Last summer he offered a prize of $5,000 for the best essay on the destruction of the spruce bud moth. Our government in New Brunswick has a very good system of. fire protection: lookout stations are established on nearly all the high mountains of the province; these are connected by telephone with headquarters in the centres of population so that forest fires may be detected in their early stages and dealt with before they spread. In that respect we are carrying on good work, but that work was started about thirty years too late. I am firmly convinced that more lumber has been .destroyed by fire in New Brunswick than has ever been cut by the woodsman's axe. The destruction of the lumber is not the only consideration; the potential value of the land for the growing of trees has' practically disappeared, due to the burning of the soil. Where the lumbermen cut over they take the larger trees; the smaller growth trees then grow more rapidly, and a crop of logs can be harvested every ten years if the cutting is judiciously done. On the other hand, spruce land which is burned over is hardly ever of any further use for the growing of trees, and that is one reason why forest fires are such a serious menace to the lumber industry.
It is also a' fact that if our forest areas become depleted there will be less moisture throughout the land. I do not need to emphasize that point so far as our friends from the prairies are concerned; where there are no forests there is little or no moisture. In eastern Canada the depletion of our forests is becoming a serious menace from this point of view; our streams are drying up;

Forest Protection

we have less moisture-less rainfall in summer and less snow in winter. Our crops are therefore in danger if we allow this depletion to continue.
The gentleman who offered the $5,000 prize for the best essay on the preservation of our forests has also offered prizes to provincial governments and private individuals for the best reforestation work in the eastern provinces, and in the carrying on of this campaign he has paid out large sums from his own private purse. I do not know what the federal government is doing at present in connection with the destruction of our forests by the spruce bud moth, but I think the Department of Agriculture could very well take under consideration the expending of some money in research work to find out if there is any possible way of combating this very destructive pest. I do not wish to detain the House at any length, but I could not let this opportunity pass without trying to impress on the House and the government the necessity of some work along this line.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. A. STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think we all agree that the forest is one of the most important sources of wealth that Canada possesses. Let me say at the outset that I am entirely in accord with the resolution. It would be a considerable impetus to the Forestry Branch of the Department of Interior to have the co-operation of the provincial authorities in the preservation of the forest wealth of the country. Anyone travelling through Canada this year could not help but be struck with the very great destruction which has resulted through forest fires. The destruction by the moth is a serious menace to the forests of eastern Canada, but probably fire is the greatest enemy we have to contend with to-day in our forests. If we were to organize from one end of Canada to the other a staff of officials who could prevent the serious destruction annually by forest fires, I do not think it would be necessary for either of my friends to make a speech urging the preservation of the forests of Canada.
I find on investigation in the Forestry branch that we are giving some attention to reforestation, but it appears to me that the thing on which we should be united, and upon which we should spend our greatest effort, both at the moment and for a considerable time to come until this menace is overcome to a very large degree, is preventing the spread of forest' fires. That is one thing we can unite upon, and that is one reason I am glad that this resolution has been introduced. Most of the provinces of Canada control their own' forests, and intervention on our part is 
more or less a matter of sufferance. I have only to say that, so far as the Department of the Interior is concerned, the Forestry branch will welcome any suggestion by which we can work in harmony with the various provinces of Canada for the preservation of the forest wealth of this country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I am not so particularly concerned about the fate of this resolution. It is a colourless, meaningless production, dealing with an important subject but in so gingerly a way that the passing of it means nothing at all. The subject, though, is of consequence and of pressing consequence. It becomes more pressing every year and I venture to say that its imperious character has not been realized by the people of Canada, and I fear I must say has not been realized by the government of Canada.
Co-operation is a word that covers a multitude of sins in these days, or rather, covers a multitude of omissions; but what is in mind when we advocate co-operation? The subject demands action; it demands a broad big policy and the inauguration of that policy now. Consequently, we should not pass lightly over a resolution of this kind without taking the occasion to press home to the government the imperative demand that such a policy be evolved.
I did not expect this discussion to be precipitated to-day. I am not prepared with the figures and the data I would like to be armed with, but I can, I think, recall enough facts to show the serious character of the position we are in, and as I do so, I am not attributing the position we are in to anyone in particular. I am not saying that governments have failed to keep up with public opinion on the question. I am saying, though, that public opinion has failed to keep up with the increasing importance of the subject from year to year, and that consequently parliament has not been alive to that importance itself. I lived for some years under the impression which I think now was a delusion, that the rate of depletion of our forest areas was not greater than the rate of accretion, that is to say, that the production from year to year was overtaking the damage by fire, the damage by disease, and, as well, the reduction by the lumber cut. I do not think there is a question of doubt that that is not only not the case, but that it is so very far from being the truth that we are rapidly approaching the end of our lumber resources.
Mr. Bamum, the gentleman who no doubt is referred to bv the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell), has produced an array of statistics and a weight of argument

Forest Protection
that it seems to me is bound to impress anyone who reads fully his production. At all events, let me say this: I have seen no answer whatever to the case Air. Bamjum presented. I have seen nothing, indeed, which detracts from the force of his contention that we are within a short time, and not a fraction of a century, but a matter of a very few years at the present rate of depletion and of cut, of the end of our forest resources. Nor have I seen his contention answered that the preservation of our forests as they are to-day, and in the extent they are to-day is vital not only to the supply of timber for our country, but vital as well to getting the real value of our agricultural and other resources in this Dominion. Our rainfall and the distribution of that rainfall is affected by the distribution of our forests, and when our forests are gone the result seems to be inevitable, that the great body of our rainfall gets off the land without adding that nutriment to the soil that comes from keeping the rainfall for a certain time within the soil itself.
There are many other consequences that follow such depletion. The contention is advanced by Mr. Bamjum that the United States of America is within a few ye^rs, indeed, less than a dozen at the present rate of consumption, of the end of its forest resources, and that Cahada, unless some policy designed to conserve those resources is adopted, is not far from that proximity to the end itself. There has been, of course we all admit, a frightful devastation by fire. There has been an almost equal devastation by the bud-worm and other destroyers of our trees. There has been also, of course, a very considerable depletion by the methods of lumber men. These are going on together, and by present means I venture to say that it is impossible to apply any adequate check. We do, of course, what we can to check the spread of fires in the western provinces -where the forests are under the control of the Dominion of Canada, but though we multiply our service to that end and add to our Forestry branch of the Interior department, and though I believe we have very expert and faithful officials, it is none the less true that as our machinery has expanded, the forest fires have expanded in almost equal degree. Coming to the other provinces we cannot apply our machinery there; we cannot apply our regulations. We suffer from that even in the west. We cannot apply them for the reason that the jurisdiction is under the provinces themselves. Consequently, the difficulties that surround the subject are many and great. They would seem indeed almost insurmountable, and I venture such suggestions as I wish to make with very considerable diffidence. But because I believe that discussion is worthless unless we come to grips with some specific idea that is worth discussion and worthy of consideration with a view of getting to some goal, I advance one. We might place the prohibition of a heavy export duty upon our pulpwood. I know there are objections to that; there are objections to every policy. In the provinces there is prohibition upon the export of pulpwood cut on provincial lands. That obtains in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, the two larger provinces of Canada. I think it obtains in other provinces as well. I know of no reason why, if that is good sound and defensible policy in relation to timber owned by the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, it would not be a reason equally effective against the exportation of pulpwood from other provinces of Canada. That it would perhaps be met by retaliatory legislation on the part of the United States is an argument which is often advanced. It is a subject that one does not care to discuss until he has viewed it from every angle, but from such study as I have been able to give I am not at all convinced that we are subject to retaliatory legislation that would put us in a position in which we would suffer as much as we are sure to suffer by the continued free exports of pulpwood. That is the suggestion that I commend to the government for its consideration.
Now, to meet another difficulty, and a bigger one, I make this suggestion: it is impossible for any province to adopt legislation looking to the safe cutting of our timber, to the clearing of the land with a view to preventing the spread of fire following the cutting of the timber, unless other provinces do the same. For example, if the province of Quebec were to consider adopting the slash clearing policy, and the province of Ontario did not follow in the same line of policy, then the lumberman of Quebec would be put at a disadvantage with his competitor that would probably be fatal to his business; consequently it follows that whatever is done of any importance to the lumber industry in this regard in one province must be accompanied by a like course in another province, or it becomes impracticable in the province that considers its adoption. Then, how can the Dominion parliament meet the situation with a view to the adoption, say of the slash clearing policy in all the provinces of Canada, because, unless we are going to insist, at whatever cost, on the clearing of the slash after the timber is felled, we simply pave the way,
Forest Protection

we feed the flames, and make all our difficulties in the way of preventing and overcoming forest fires in the future. Well, there are two or three ways in which that can be done-[DOT] two or three, at all events, worth trying. The provinces might be brought together and we might perhaps agree with the government? of those provinces to recommend to their several legislatures the adoption of uniform regulations in this regard. I question if that would succeed. It might succeed and it might not, but if everything should fail it would be at least possible for this Dominion, and in my judgment it would be not only constitutionally practical but would be justified by the stern necessity, to make the failure to clear slash in the public interest an offence by Dominion legislation, and to make it compulsory upon all private operators in timber and on our timber land. If that were done, then unquestionably it should be followed by operators upon public lands in the various provinces.
The hon. member lefers to the burning of slash?
Yes, I refer to that.

Does the hon. member realize that our spruce in eastern Canada grows from a tree the size of your arm to trees of very large size, and it is impossible to burn the slash without killing the small growth?

No, I do not think it is impossible, without killing the small growth. I know it grows in that way. If the slash is killed by fire wherever it lies, necessarily that would ensue, but it would be quite possible to have regulations that would provide for the gathering or the accumulation of slash, and then provide that it would be got out of the way in some manner, and I presume, of course, by fire, and thereby take away the main cause of the spread of forest fires in future. I for one can see no way in the world in which we can ensure ourselves against the spread of these large forest fires that are devastating the great wealth of the country unless we take away the fuel of these flames. It is this fuel that causes the flames to spread. It is that which starts them going, and though it be a matter of expense, the extent of that expense is already pretty well known. That it does cost something to accumulate and to bum this slash without at the same time destroying the young growth is now pretty well established but it is far better that that cost be borne, and added, indeed, to the cost of our lumber-for there is where it is going to come-than that we
(Mr. Meighen.]
now should not only mortgage prosperity to pursue blindly and prodigally a policy that is going to leave the country depleted of not only one of its great sources of its wealth, but of one of those sources that is vital to the other sources, without which the main source at all events is of very little value, to our land.

speakeroldname: Mr. MURRAY MacLAREN (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
It is a matter of general agreement that our forest lands are becoming unduly and greatly depleted. There are three causes for the depletion of our forests-fire, insect diseases, end overcutting. All are important factors. They may vary somewhat in degree, but they are all formidable and large factors in the depletion. The depletion of our forests is a serious matter for the country's welfare, not only on account of the enormous wealth that is being lost, but because the replacement of the forests requires so many years. It is appreciated now-and I do not think we need take an absolutely dark view as regards our forest lands in this respect-that general knowledge is now being diffused throughout the land regarding the serious conditions that exist, and what steps should be taken to prevent it. That of itself is something. It has not reached the point where action is being taken to nearly the extent that it should be taken. It is becoming recognized now that the condition of our forests is somewhat similar to the condition of health in the human being-that there is such a thing as forest health and such a thing as forest disease, and that when forest disease occurs our forests suffer to a very great extent. What causes forest disease? There are two principal causes. One is fire and the other is overcutting. Fire destroys a large portion of the forest and the soil; it lowers the health of the region and encourages, just as is the case in human diseases-the onset and growth of insect disease. In the same way over-cutting encourages plant disease. If forests are overcut,, the land dries, the trees die, the high state of health of the forest depreciates, and this allows the onset of insect and lower animal life disease. These are matters of importance for our people to know, so that the problem may be dealt with, with a reasonable hope of success.
What can be done to solve this great and serious economic problem in Canada? I should be disposed to attach a good deal more value to the word "co-operation" than I have so far heard mentioned. And why? Forest lands are the property of the provinces, and the federal government has a Department of Agriculture. This, then, must largely be a

Forest Protection
matter of co-operation between the provincial governments and the federal government, and much could be gained by a series of conferences between the federal government, especially its Department of Agriculture, and the local governments. To what effect? So that they would agree and lay down certain standards-what measures should be adopted for the prevention of fire? How should we deal with the removal- of slash? To what extent should we attempt to keep our forests clean? How should we deal with insect diseases? It has been mentioned that we must look to the federal Department of Agriculture for more assistance, because they have the entomologists who are carrying on this work. The federal government might help us still further in the matter of plant pathology, in view of the fact that forest diseases are so destructive to our forest life at the present time. We have now reached the point where our forests have suffered so severly that we must have recourse to those measures, and we must preserve our forests and keep them cleaner. We might well turn our eyes towards the condition of forests in France; and if we follow the example of French forestry, where everything is carried out so completely as regards care, cutting, fire protection and removal of slash, this will be very much to our advantage. I quite recognize that this is a matter of process of time. When Canada was a new country, forests were regarded, and we regard them still somewhat, as something to be used without any sense of discrimination or limitation. That time has gone. We must now accustom ourselves to caring for our forests as is being done at the present day in France where the forests are older, the problem larger and greater care required.

Mr. Speaker, I believe the federal government should at once take measures to co-operate at least with the Ontario and Quebec governments on account of conditions which at present exist in the northern country. The discovery of gold in Rouyn township, which largely adjoins the boundary of the province of Ontario, has caused a tremendous rush of propectors into that section of northern Ontario. Within the last six or eight months, some twelve or fifteen hundred mining claims have been recorded in the township of Rouyn and adjoining townships. During the coming summer, in conformity with regulations imposed by Ontario and regulations imposed by Quebec, a certain amount of development work will have to be done upon those mining claims. Any of us who are familiar with conditions in Cobalt or in the Porcupine country, knows what happens after prospectors have gone into the bush. The slash may not be as great as that produced by lumbering; but as soon as prospecting and development work starts on a large scale, in a timber country, the same conditions are created that slash creates in a lumbering country. The section of the north country in which these mining claims have been recorded adjoins the largest and most valuable standing pulpwood there is on the North American continent, and in its present location and owing to its density, should a fire, such as the one we had in Porcupine in 1916, start in the slash that will be created in the township of Rouyn and in the district of Kirkland Lake, there will be a repetition of the great conflagration that took place in the Porcupine district and one which will cause Canada one of its greatest losses in its pulp-wood wealth. These conditions are being created; we are having to-day a repetition of what took place in the Porcupine country, and nothing less than immediate co-operation between the federal government and the governments of Ontario and Quebec will prevent a serious conflagration in the pulpwood limits of northern Ontario and Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, coming as I do from one of the greatest lumber manufacturing centres in Canada, I feel that I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without saying a few words in commendation of the spirit which prompted the mover of this resolution in bringing this matter before the House. We do not spend enough time in discussing our natural resources, in endeavouring to plan ways by which those resources may be conserved and made use of to best advantage for the people. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has quite properly stated that one of the greatest dangers to our timber is fire. I know that is true in* British Columbia. Fire has taken an immense toll of our timber and our trees, and I am afraid it is a very difficult problem to determine the best method of protecting our trees against fire. In this connection, I might mention that in Vancouver there is an air station which is maintained, I think, by the Dominion government. A very splendid work has been done by that station in patrolling the forests of British Columbia. There is an extensive territory to be covered and it is impossible in any other way properly to patrol the forests of that province. Where fires have got under way in the forests of British Columbia it is almost impossible to put them out, and what we
Forest Protection

have to do if possible is to prevent them from getting a start. That is what these men are doing. I think they have accomplished a great deal of good and I should be very sorry indeed to hear that there was any proposal to do away with this air station. I have heard it suggested that in the execution of a policy of economy, this service was going to be dispensed with or curtailed. That, I think, would be a mistake. There is no doubt about the importance of our practising economy, but it would be false economy to dispense with, or even to curtail, the air patrol which has done such splendid work in connection with the forests of British Columbia. We must realize that it has taken many hundreds of years to produce the trees that are now standing out there on the Pacific coast. I am told that some of these trees have been a thousand years growing. Now, if a tree of that kind should be destroyed by fire, and if we have to wait another thousand years-
We will not wait.

-until another one grows, it can be seen what a hopeless outlook there is if some effective means are not taken to prevent fires. I have listened with a great deal of interest to what the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has said in reference to the burning of slashings. I am afraid, however, that in British Columbia that would be a great undertaking. It would be a considerable problem to dispose of the limbs that come from one of these giant timbers; I do not know that it would be practicable in our part of the country.

I would inform the hon. member that it is not only practicable but it is being' done to-day in British Columbia.
Mr. <(VfcQUARRIE: To some extent.
Very largely.

Should not the province have the right to compel the man who cuts timber on Crown lands to clean up the slashings? He should be made to clean up these slashings at the end of each season and to prove that he has done so. His business is a profitable one and therefore he ought to be made to clean up.

I accept the assurance of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) as to the practicability of this proposal. Of soiirse, if it can be carried out it is something that certainly should be done. I thought, how-[DOT]evet, that it presented a rather big problem.
tMr. McQuarrie.]
I think we should make every effort possible to conserve our timber wealth because it is one of the greatest assets we have. In my district we are to-day shipping lumber to a great many parts of the world. The business is almost wholly an export one, and if it had not been for the timber industry in British Columbia during the last few years I am afraid that province would not be in the satisfactory position it* occupies to-day. We are doing a world trade in lumber, and as I see it, we have only just started; there is a great future ahead of us. Our timber seems to be unlimited in extent. But unless we take every precaution to protect it from the ravages of fire, I fear it will be sadly depleted. I am very strongly in favour of bringing such matters to the attention of the House and I commend the action of the hon. member (Mr. Michaud) in moving his resolution.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have been very much pleased to notice from several quarters in the House the commendation of the good work that Mr. Frank Barnjum is doing in educating the Canadian people on this very important subject. Mr. Barnjum is a Canadian who spent some years in the United States, prosperous years I am glad to know, and has now returned to Canada filled with splendid enthusiasm and prepared to do whatever is possible for the promotion of every Canadian industry. He feels a deep interest in this subject because he has been associated with the business for a long time. Everything that he proposes in the way of forest conservation, every movement that can be made for the better protection of the forests from fires, everything that can be done in the way of tree planting, and all that Mr. Barnjum desires in the interests of our forests, will, I am sure, have the heartiest sympathy of the House and the public generally. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) said he had had a revelation in regard to the alleged endless valuable forests of Canada. I had a somewhat similar experience. I am reminded that very many years ago, travelling in Nova Scotia in the southern portion of the province,
I had the pleasure of meeting an old Scotsman who was engaged in the lumber business. He had carried on operations in Sweden, Norway, I think, Newfoundland and then in Nova Scotia, and he seemed to have a grievance. Meeting a minister he naturally wanted to air his grievance. He said he had a great complaint to make, because we were charging him a duty on seeds. I said I did not think that the duty on seeds was very high and I did not think that his grievance could be very

Forest Protection
grave. I asked him what kind of seeds they were. Spruce seeds, he said. As we looked out of the window of the train we saw a thick spruce forest. "What are you talking about spruce trees for?" I asked him. " Why, there is any quantity of spruce trees in the province." In his broadest Scotch he said: "Mr. Fielding,
I give you warning that if there is not a policy of tree planting in Nova Scotia and in this country generally, and in America, within twenty-five years there will be a timber famine in Canada and on the American continent." Well, ten or twelve years passed, and very much of what the old gentleman predicted had come true. At that time he was planting trees. My right hon. friend was substantially, though not technically, correct in his reference to the provincial regulations; and he apparently suggested that what was good enough for Quebec and Ontario was good enough for ' the other provinces. He rather assumed that there was a prohibition on the export of wood in these provinces. That is not technically correct, although in the main it is. Neither the province of Ontario nor the province of Quebec has the power to prohibit the export of wood or to impose an export duty. But in Ontario and Quebec the provincial governments are owners of timber lands. They lease timber lands to people desiring to operate them; and any landlord who has any land to lease can impose any condition he desires on the lessee. So that the fact is that in the province of Quebec and in the province of Ontario the export of wood is largely, though not absolutely, prohibited in its raw state. But it is not correct to assume that this prohibition is general, because one of the difficulties is in relation to private lands. My good friend Mr. Barnjum is enthusiastic in all these movements and he goes further than any one who has spoken on this subject. He attaches great importance to the entire prohibition of the export of wood. Perhaps a high export duty might serve the same purpose, but he insists that the export of wood should not be allowed at all. It so happens that there are lands in Quebec that are not owned by the government but by private persons, and no prohibition	can be	applied	to _ them.
On private lands the'man who can raise pulp-wood thinks he has the same right to handle it as the man who raises any other crop. We heard a good deal on that question years ago in the course of a tariff investigation. At that time the owners of private lands complained very bitterly against any prohibition or restriction being put upon the export of their wood, and they stated that this would be equivalent to placing them at the mercy
of a few home manufacturers. I am not adopting one view or the other, I am merely repeating the objections urged on that occa. sion.
My right hon. friend mentioned retaliation by the United States, and that means a great deal. I am very much impressed myself by the letters Mr. Bamjum has written, and I know he has educated a great many people on the importance of this subject. I must admit that I have at times entertained a considerable measure of sympathy with his proposal that we should absolutely prohibit export, but there are grave difficulties in the way, and anyone who comes from forest districts, notably those in the province of Quebec, where timber areas are in private hands, will see at once that the prohibition or restriction of export would probably create a good deal of ill-feeling. My sympathies go largely to Mr. Barnjum, and perhaps in a little while we shall be able to find a solution of the problem. Meanwhile I think my hon. friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud) has done good service in raising this discussion to-day.

Mr. Speaker, most of this discussion has been confined to districts where lumbering operations have been in progress, and there the slash is no doubt a menace. But I have travelled hundreds of miles through forests in which no cutting has ever been done, and there I found the marks of fire. I saw now and again lying on the ground the tranks of trees three feet in diameter, which is pretty big for spruce, and I do not believe anything but fire has destroyed what must at one time have been very heavy forest growth. On the edge of these forests one can see where settlers have cut down trees, but as the greater portion of the area belongs to the Dominion government, comparatively little interference has taken place.
I think the resolution is appropriate in calling for co-operation between the Dominion government and the governments of the several provinces to ensure protection of our forest reserves against fire. At one time I was under the, impression that Canada had unlimited forest wealth, but since going through various forest areas I have come to the conclusion that there is a limit in this respect unless we stop the ravages of fire.
As to placing an embargo on the export of forest products, I do not see that that would help at all in the part of the country to which I am referring, because it has never been possible, so far, to do any cutting there on a commercial scale. But those forest areas are
Canadian Magazines

worth protecting, and we should educate the people on the importance of co-operating in this national work. No doubt considerable damage has been caused by insects, but I am not well enough acquainted with the actual conditions to speak definitely on this point. It is my opinion, however, that in the wilder lands to which I am referring very little damage has been caused by the depredations of insects; most of it is attributable to fire.
I think this resolution will have a good effect by impressing on the people the need of fire protection if we are to preserve our forest wealth. I agree with my hon. friend from British Columbia (Mr. McQuarrie) that the aeroplane is the best means of patrolling our forests, for it affords better observation and enables fires to be reported very shortly after they break out, and that is the time we must get after them and control them. Therefore I think the air service is indispensable in taking care of most of our forests outside the settled areas.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (West Toronto) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of thia House, it is desirable that measures should be adopted to encourage the publication of Canadian magazines and periodicals. .
He said: Mr. Speaker, my purpose in presenting this resolution is to bring to the attention of the House the very grievous state of an important industry-one which is not only an industry in the ordinary sense of the word, but is a factor in the education of our peoples as well as an important agent in the development of our national life.
We talk of the publishing industry as we would of any other manufacturing industry, but, Mr. Speaker, it is something more than that. The periodical press of a country is an educational institution, and in every country where there has been created and developed a good periodical press, there you will find the national ideals more firmly established and the unity of the people brought about in the most satisfactory. manner.
We have a very difficult country in which to establish national unity: we have many racial problems and we have also the problems of geography. In addition to the two chief racial groups, there are in western Canada a great many colonies of people who still cherish the ideals of their native countries and seek to perpetuate their old national customs. Unless we can bring these people

into harmony with the rest of the country we will never establish that national unity which is so desirable. And I maintain, Sir, that one of the most, if not the most, effective agency is the publication of magazines and periodicals with a nation-wide circulation.
In addition to these racial impediments that afflict our country, there are geographical difficulties to overcome in establishing our national ideals and in promoting the harmony of the people. There are the differences of material interests between the Maritime provinces, and Quebec and Ontario; and still further differences of material interests between the Maritime provinces and the western provinces. To make the sentiment of one province known to another becomes a great national service and a great national duty which we should use every available agency to promote.
The diversity of material interests between the Far East and the Far West, in the absence of some means of communication that will bring them closer together, is one of the reasons why there has been so much misunderstanding between their respective inhabitants. I believe that notwithstanding anything that has been said in the West or in the East, there exists in every province a keen desire to assist every other province in achieving that degree of prosperity for which it strives. There is more Canadian spirit in the Dominion, I think, than most of us realize, but it is necessary that it should be made coherent and that it should be understood in the different sections of the country. We all know how proud the East is of the West, of its great productiveness and of the virility of its people; and we know that the West, notwithstanding that you do not hear very much of it on the platform or in the press, has more admiration for the enterprise of the East than perhaps is apparent to those who look upon the matter superficially. But to many it is hard to discover a way for the East and the West to co-operate in national policies to the advantage of both the grand divisions of the country.
It is unavoidable, Sir, in a country with so large an area as ours, embracing, as it does, three thousand miles of territory, that what is closest to us bulks most largely, the result being that local interests in the different sections have more prominence in the minds of the people than the national interests. To this must be attributed any provincial jealousies that may exist. I think it is the duty of government, by just and equitable laws, to convince the people in all sections that their welfare is the deep concern of the

Canadian Magazines
administration. I think it can be said that that duty has been had in mind by every government we have had in Canada. Errors in judgment have been committed; there have been errors of policy on trade questions, on transportation questions and on many other matters, but it has always been the intention of the governments of Canada to serve the interests of the whole people. This parliament must view public questions in a broader way than they are looked at in many of the provinces where local interests bulk so largely. If, therefore, we are to bring the people together it is imperative that all the agencies available to secure this end should be employed to the fullest measure.
Now, among the agencies to promote national ideals and advance national unity, I think the press is the most effective. In my judgment the daily press cannot perform this work. It suffers from two disabilities. First, the daily press is partisan; secondly, its circulation is local, or at the widest, provincial. The editors of daily papers must cater to their respective constituencies; what affects parts of the country remote from the place of publication is treated very lightly or in some cases gets no attention at all, thus local feeling is stimulated and national considerations are overlooked. I am not attempting, Sir, to discredit or belittle the daily press. He would be a very injudicious person who would attempt to do that, because we know the mighty place it occupies in this or any other democracy. But I am trying to point out that the exigencies of the business of running a daily newspaper make it pretty nearly impossible for that newspaper to take the national as opposed to the local or provincial viewpoint on many questions. There is, therefore, in my opinion, a definite and very important field for magazines and periodicals. I am not insensible of the fact that these might show bias or partisanship, but the success of a publisher would depend upon the absence of such bias or partisanship; he must first consider the requirements from the business standpoint, and the danger of bias and partisanship is likely to be very slight. If, then, there is to be an independent press to express the sentiment of all Canada, it must be found in the periodical press and the magazines of the country. Canadian periodicals, which are all too few in number and have circulations all too small, have the ability to interpret the sentiment of one province to the other-the sentiment of the Maritime provinces to British Columbia, to Alberta, Saskatchewan or Ontario, and the sentiment of those provinces, then, to the
East. No daily newspaper can do that; no daily newspaper has a circulation covering the different provinces. This service, therefore, can be rendered only by a virile, profitable and successful magazine press. To bring the East and the West together for their mutual understanding on great national issues would be a patriotic service of no small moment, but it can be performed only by publications having, as I say, a nation-wide circulation. Only by such publications can we ever hope to develop Canadian national ideals, to create a market for the productions of Canadian writers, and provide for those opportunities to use their talents for the dissemination of Canadian literature throughout the whole Dominion. That is a legitimate field for the efforts of publishers.
Nothing more surely conduces to national pride than a national literature. I think it can be said that Canada to-day cannot claim to have a national literature in the shape of a periodical press such as prevails in the Mother Country and in the republic to the south. There is no young country in the world which has so much material for good writers, so much romance mixed with its history, as this .Dominion of Canada. The discovery of the country; the work of the early pioneers who hewed out their homes from the dense forest; the intrepidity of the officers and servants of the Hudson's Bay Company; the wonderful exploits of the Northwest Mounted Police- these are just a few of the things which writers could discuss for the entertainment and benefit of Canada and for the development of our national literature.
The trouble to-day, Sir, is that Canada is being Americanized by the periodicals of the United States-a process which is proceeding much more rapidly than is realized by the average citizen who does not give a great deal of study to the question. If it were the best class of American magazines that had the largest circulation in this country there would not be so much ground for complaint, but such magazines as Harper's, Scribner's and others of the same class have comparatively limited, indeed, extremely limited, circulation in this country, while those like the Red Book, Snappy Stories and that kind of stuff-
Snappy Stories has been banned.
It does not circulate any more in Canada?
It ought not to.

I agree with the Minister
of Customs (Mr. Bureau). There are other

Canadian Magazines
magazines that may have not so "snappy" a name but have stores .that are just as "snappy" as those that appear in Snappy Stories. I hope my hon. friend will ban that new magazine which I will refer to in a moment.
The adolescent mind of Canada is being trained by a long catalogue of frothy and frequently anti-British and often suggestive writing that should be discouraged. I am glad to hear from the Minister of Customs that he is banning this kind of stuff as he discovers it. This kind of literature is specially favoured in being introduced into this country, and that is the bone of contention that I am endeavouring to present. I do not think that we should continue to allow the mental pabulum of the youth of this country to be the Yellow Kid and Mr. Jiggs and other stuff sent out by the Hearst Syndicate. How can we hope to nourish the intellectuality of our young men and young women by suck puerility as we see in the syndicated stuff and in the magazine and other periodical publications that fill the news stands of this country.
I was interested the other day in reading a pamphlet on Canadian Literature of French Expression by Jules Tremblay, and in it I find this which I would like to present to the House as the opinion of an author of some prominence in this part of the country. Referring to the Americanization of this country through the periodical press, he says:
All our provinces hold certain things in common. One, considered dangerous, is the peaceful; an<l steady intrusion of Americanism through the stage, the wireless, the moving picture shows, the phonograph, the magazine, certain newspaper services, and the book. American ideas permeate our minds to-day. No reason there were to complain, did we borrow from our neighbours their qualities with their goods. But people, as a rule, rather borrow defects, faults, and vices, or indispensable things from other races. Our idiosyncracies are adjudged too slow, and must be replaced by fashions of speech, dress, dancing, and thoughtless libertism in matters of religion. . . . Do you not think that this easy going penetration will never promote the best kind of nationalism in Canada? I bear no preconceived hostility against Americans. I have lived long enough with them to know their real worth. But we do not import too much of their worth. The brand of accessions that comes from them to us is a source of alarm for Canadian unity. Segregation is in the air, not far from the Rockies; it is potential only, just now, but may very soon become actual, if we do not find a strong counterpart; and that counterpart is Canadianism opposed to Americanism. We must shape our own destinies for ourselves, and not for outsiders. Unless we act with a purpose, we are of small account in the process of change. In twenty-five years, we may be Canadians in name and Americans in fact, a fact which may politically evolve a few decades later.
Evolution is constant. Canada will be transformed, with the rest of the world. The surviving nations will be those where the people will have kept faith with their own traditions; and these traditions are best maintained by literature, by national literature.

I entirely agree with Mr. Tremblay, and I quote his words as those of a man who has given a great deal of thought to this particular subjept.
Before going on I would like to quote a paragraph taken from the Ottawa Citizen of February 24. Referring to the address given by Colonel R. H. Webb at the Carnegie Library, it says:
He said that one or two United States firms alone were selling upwards of $38,000,000 worth of American books in Canada. [DOT]
I know that the copyright law has a great deal to do with that, but I think it is fair to say that the taste that is being developed in Canada by these American periodicals is also largely to blame for that tremendously large importation of American books. What I venture to say is that w;e should make an effort to give every reasonable encouragement to the men who are willing to risk their means and devote their business ability to providing a substitute for this overwhelming mass oi American literature that is coming into this country. At least, we should be willing to remove the handicaps, the unfair competition under which the publishers of our magazines and periodicals labour at the present time.
I happen to know of many men who at different times have endeavoured to establish Canadian national- publications. I have watched them organize their forces, launch their enterprises and carry them on until they had sunk perhaps one or two or three hundred thousand dollars, and then be forced to suspend publication. That has been the experience of the great majority of those who have ever attempted to organize a Canadian periodical press. They have almost all met with disaster. There is only one publication in Canada to-day that has a circulation of 75,000. There never was but one that had a circulation of over 100,000, and that one.
1 understand, has recently suspended publication. So that it is not that Canadians have lacked the enterprise. It is not altogether the fact that they have neglected what may bf called the duty of trying to develop a Canadian literature through the periodical press, because many of them have tried, have used up all their resources, and finally have had to desist.
The extent to which American magazines come into Canada is not generally understood, nor is the very rapid increase that is taking place in that importation. People in the ordinary course of their business see the bookstalls filled with flashy covers, but they do not take the time, perhaps they have not got the time, to get the facts as to the

Canadian Magazines
-quantity of this material that is coming in or as to its character. It may surprise some members of this House to know that for every Canadian periodical sold in this country there are four American publications sold; that is to say, that by reason of the handicaps under v.'hich this particular industry is suffering Canadian publishers are able to secure only twenty per cent of their home market. There is no other industry operating in this country that could possibly exist under conditions of that kind, or that could even -get capital to start under such conditions, and the situation for the Canadian publisher is getting worse every year. I have a memorandum prepared by the Canadian National Newspaper and Periodical Association, and it presents a few figures which 1 think it would be well to put on Hansard. In 1912 the total value of the magazines coming into this country was $831,000 and in 1922 the value was $3,122,000. In ten years the volume of American periodicals coming into Canada increased from $831,000 to over $3,000,000. That will indicate the rapidity of the growth that has taken place in the last ten years, and the conditions are so favourable to American publishers and so difficult for Canadian publishers that this increase is likely to continue in proportion as our population grows. Owing to the conditions under which the business in foreign publications is carried on in Canada there has been a growth in ten years from $800,000 to over $3,000,000.
Now, Sir, the meretricious charcter of most of those publications is something that should give the people of this country concern, especially those who are interested in the moral welfare of the people, particularly the young people. They are devoted almost entirely to . fiction of a most sensationally suggestive and generally demoralizing character-about as demoralizing in some cases as publishers dare print. I noticed recently in an Ottawa paper the advertisement of a new magazine called, The True Story Magazine. Here it is. Hon. members may have noticed the advertisements. It has been printed all the way across Canada, and it is a pretty fair sample of the kind of stuff the American publishers are sending in for the young people of this country. I see here the statement " Has every man and woman a soul mate?" Perhaps we ought to have a sole mate, but not this kind of soul mate. This advertisement sets out this kind of stuff as an inducement for the young people of this country to buy the paper. One of the stories they print is headed " Whose Daughter ", and it goes on to give a brief description of the story. It says:
Suppose your own sister turned out to be "the other woman." Suppose your husband frankly told of his love for her, and showed a revulsion to yourself to whom he was married; suppose a love child was born to your, sister, your husband its father, and during the birth your sister died. Would you adopt the child and bring it up?
And so on. Is that the kind of stuff to be allowed to come into the Dominion of Canada under specially favourable conditions? This is a new magazine. Perhaps the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) when he reads some of these stories may ban this magazine, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a class of literature such as this should be prevented from coming in, and that steps should be taken to encourage a wholesome literature such as Canadian publishers will produce if they have an opportunity and a fair chance of making ends meet.
I am going to give the House some reasons why Canadian publishers are unable to compete. In the first place the raw materials of the Canadian publisher are taxed, and that leaves him at a very serious disadvantage with his competitor in the United States. He has to pay in Canada for white paper a price equivalent to the United States price plus the duty.

Will the hon. member explain why it is we have to import the white
magazine paper from the United States, when we are large exporters of white paper?

We do not have to import the white paper, but white paper is sold in the United States at 25 per cent less than in Canada. It is sold at an advance greater than 25 per cent, because you pay for Canadian paper exactly what you would pay for paper bought in the United States, plus the duty and plus the freight.

I am informed-and the hon. member will know whether my information is correct or not-that the character of paper that goes into magazines is not manufactured here, that it is an American manufacture and that the quantity that is used here would not warrant the manufacture in this country. Newsprint is another paper ' altogether and of course we manufacture that.

The information given to the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is not correct. There are a good many book paper mills in this country doing quite an extensive business. There is a mill at Georgetown and mills at other places. Book paper of all grades is manufactured in Canada, but it is sold in the United States for 25 per cent less than in Canada. The same is
Canadian Magazines

true of engravings, inks and other raw materials that go into the production of magazines. There is protection for the papermaker, the inkmaker and the engraver, and everybody else that produces anything that goes into the magazine, excepting printing presses, and there is no duty on them because they are not made in Canada. If that were the only handicap it would be bad enough, but there are other factors more serious than that. So far as the Canadian circulation is concerned, the American publisher has an enormous advantage. In his own country he sells anywhere from	50,000 to	2,000,000 copies
of an issue, it may be a weekly or it may be a monthly. What he sells in the United States pays all the cost of overhead, typesetting, proof-reading, making of plates, engraving and everything. These charges amount, I should say, to about 80 per cent of the total cost of producing a magazine, and they are all met by the domestic circulation. So that all the cost the publisher has to meet for his Canadian circulation is that of Iris white paper and press work, and the freight charges incurred in sending the product to Canada. Once a magazine is prepared for the press the cost of running off a few extra thousand copies for Canada is only a very small proportion of the total expense. He dumps into Canada his excess circulation, and thereby makes it impossible for the Canadian publishers to establish Canadian periodicals. Besides that, many of these publications that are coming in are unfit for young people to read. The Canadian publisher has to meet all this competition.
Let me for a moment put the matter in this way. Take the cost of writing, editing, type-setting, for a circulation, we will say, of
50.000	in Canada and compare that with similar cost for a publication in the United States with a circulation of 50,000 in Canada, and you will see how much greater the overhead is of any publisher who is trying to do business in Canada. As I said before, I know of only one Canadian publication that ever reached a circulation of 100,000, and that publication reached that circulation by methods of puzzles and guesses and that kind of thing. That was not a healthy, normal circulation; but even that publication has gone out of business; it has recently ceased publishing. Any Canadian publisher who is able to secure
50.000	circulation is regarded as a very successful man, but there are scores of American publications selling in Canada 50,000 copies, all the cost of which to the publisher is the white paper, the press work and the freight. I contend that conditions which make it possible for foreign publishers to secure a

wider circulation in Canada of their publications than can be gained by their Canadian competitors call for amendment. Under present conditions, a Canadian publisher would be at an advantage if he put up a plant in Buffalo or Detroit. He would get his paper at nearly 30 per cent less, and he would have the advantage of a certain circulation in the United States. In fact, I know of one publisher in my own city who, a few years ago, seriously considered moving his printing plant to Buffalo. If he had, perhaps he would be in business yet. He did not take that step, and he is now one of the "has-beens"; he is one of those who have had, during the last few years, to suspend publication.
What would be the effect of the abolition of the duty on these book papers?

Not very much. I think conditions call for greater amendment than that. Twenty-five per cent reduction on the paper would be something, because paper is a big item in periodical publications; but the biggest item is the writing and, of course, that would not be affected. Something more than that is necessary if Canadian publishers are ever going to be able to establish Canadian publications.
Present conditions are unfair to employees as well as to employers. I know of one publisher in this country who circulates about
75,000	magazines, who pays in wages $125,000 a year. If the 1,183,000 copies of American publications that come in here every month were produced by the workmen of the Dominion, there would be fifteen times as much paid in wages in this industry in Canada. If American publishers were put on a fair basis of competition with Canadian publishers, many of the former might find it profitable to print in Canada, and that would add to the volume of work for Canadian workmen. Our friends in the United States take very good care to guard their American workmen when the question is one of publication of books or anything under the Copyright Act. Nobody can get a copyright for a book in the United States until the type is set up and the book produced in the United States. If we followed that plan and required books and magazines to be set up in this country, of course that would be prohibition. I am not arguing for that; I do not think we need go that far; but I want to point out that there is a real market in Canada for periodical literature, as is proved by the fact that 15,000,000 copies of American magazines are sold annually in this country. If we could secure half the volume of that trade, it would mean a large expen-

Canadian Magazines
diture of money in wages as well as making the industry somewhat profitable for those who engage in it. I have questioned some men who are in this line of business, and they estimate that, with proper encouragement, there would be a potential extension of this business to, at least, $10,000,000 a year; that is, this would be an industry expending $10,000,000 a year in Canada. I am giving that only as an estimate; but undoubtedly the industry would be very greatly expanded if it were possible to continue on any reasonable basis of profit.
All kinds of magazines are coming into Canada; but as the present leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) said last year, prime objection is to be taken to American Sunday School publications that come in. I have no objection to the morality of their teachings, but these papers are edited for American children. All their illustrations are drawn from the lives of the great men of the republic. All their heroes and heroines are Americans. The whole atmosphere of those papers is that of the United States. We should remember that these papers are perused by very young children. At the beginning of their lives, they are taught American ideas instead of Canadian ideas, and this prepares them, as they grow a little older, to take up with those meretricious American magazines that come in so freely, and to make them the chief source of their mental exercise. Are we not perpetuating conditions that are calculated to Americanise our Dominion and to prevent the development of a strong Canadian sentiment, when we begin with little children going to Sunday school, and follow that up with Snappy Pictures, and True Stories and the rest of it as the children grow to young manhood and young womanhood, until they are fed on that kind of stuff and nothing else and rarely read good books that are available. Their taste is vitiated; they are unable to value and appreciate good literature.
I am not proposing that a subsidy should be granted to magazines. At the present time this government grants an annual subsidy of $50,000 a year to the daily press to assist them in carrying on a news-gathering service. That has been paid, I think, for at least three or four years. Therefore, even if the periodical press asked for a subsidy, it would have a good precedent for doing so. I think that money spent on the daily press is well spent; but if it is good policy to give substantial financial assistance to the daily press, would it not be equally sound policy to remove the handicaps from which our periodical press suffers?
To my mind, having in view the value of developing a national literature and building up strong Canadian sentiment, the case for the periodical press is stronger than that for the daily press.
I should like to submit to the House another aspect of this question, and while it may be thought that I am straining the case a little.
I do not think I am. What effect have these American publications on the movement of population? How far do they account for the emigration of so many of our people to the United States? What part do they play in making it hard for us to keep our young people here? There is nothing we want in this country more than population; the government spends large sums of money in order to get people here, and yet our population increases much more slowly than it should. I think we may trace this directly to the large emigration to the United States. We bring people in, they live here for a short time, and then drift across the line. They would not go there unless they felt that the opportunities there were better. And how do they get that idea? I do not think they get it from the daily press of the country in the particular localities in which they live. My contention is that they get it from the reading of American periodicals. The United States is pictured to them as a land of greater opportunity. Not deliberately perhaps, but none the less actively, those periodicals carry on a propaganda which finally convinces thousands of our best young people, the most enterprising and virile, that while they may get a living in Canada they would do very much better in the United States. When that kind of thing is read week after week and month after month by young men and women it is bound to have its effect.
There is no counter-irritant, so to speak. No publications are put into their hands to show them that there - are counter attractions in Canada, because it is impossible for our publishers to compete in the volume of reading matter provided or the number of copies distributed. We can have no complaint to make if our young people slip across the line believing they can meet with better opportunities in the United States. We know as a fact that they can have no better opportunity there than in Canada, but the Canadian opportunities are not set out in the same striking and attractive way. That is what should be done in this country, and any agency that can and will do that should have the favourable consideration of the government. In fact, we need a little Canadian propaganda; at any rate we need fair statements as to the pos-

sibility of achieving success in our country. The Consul General of the United States in his report says:
To a large extent the Canadian reader of magazines depends upon those published in the United States, The advertisements in these magazines are perused with considerable advantage to the advertiser, as they keep before the public numerous lines of American merchandise.
I want to refer for a moment or two to the unfairness to the Canadian manufacturer in American magazines being able to present the claims of his competitors so freely and extensively in a medium from which he is excluded. All this publicity which the American magazines afford in Canada to the extent of
1,183,000	copies a month is denied to the Canadian manufacturer because it is absolutely beyond his reach to get it. Space in these magazines is sold on a basis of the total circulation, which runs to hundreds of thousands and in some cases to millions of each issue. Ninety per cent of that being in the United States and ten per cent in Canada, manifestly the Canadian manufacturer cannot get his announcements published in these magazines; he has to pay for two millions of circulation in order to reach 100,000 readers. There is one magazine in the United States which circulates in this country to the extent of 95,000 odd and its advertising charges are $7,000 a page. If the Canadian manufacturer tried to get into that magazine he would have to pay $7,000 a page for a circulation of 100,000,-some thing so preposterous that no one would consider it for a moment. But all his competitors in the United States advertise their goods in this country to 100.000 readers and it costs them nothing more than what they pay for their American circulation. In other words, this i3 excess circulation dumped into Canada after the American edition of the magazine is printed.
I do not know whether I.am able to impress my hon. friends sufficiently with this aspect of the question. There are many articles of merchandise which could not be sold at all without large and extensive advertising; many depend entirely on advertising. And when we maintain a condition of affairs in this country that prevents our manufacturers from presenting their goods to the public of Canada on equal terms with foreign manufacturers I think we are depriving them of something that they ought to have; we are setting up conditions about which they have a right to complain. In this way our own manufacturers are more seriously handicapped than I can describe in their own home market. They have it invaded under conditions with

which they cannot compete, and this reacts on their employees, lessening the volume of output and thus effecting an increased cost of what is produced. If a man produces a magazine in this country and his circulation is only 50,000 he has to charge twice as much for the magazine as he would if he sold
150,000	copies. All his overhead costs have to be covered by the 50,000, and if he had three times that sum his overhead cost would be only one-third as much per copy. That is a very serious side of this question.
I have had put into my hand a considerable list of resolutions passed by various bodies in this country advocating that some action be taken to encourage Canadian magazines. I have a number of them here, and while I will not take up the time of the House reading them all, perhaps one or two might be worth while considering. For example, here is one passed by the Toronto Women's Liberal Association.
Hear, hear.
That is an influential body.

This resolution reads:
Whereas the number and circulation of periodicals publishing immoral and indecent reading matter is rapidly on the increase:
Be it resolved that the Toronto Women's Liberal Association do strongly urge the appointment of a national censor board to inspect all printed matter in circulation in Canada, and that copies be sent to the Minister of Customs, the Postmaster General and the Finance Minister, enclosing samples of objectionable literature.
Here is a resolution by the Canadian
Authors' Association:
Whereas, the Canadian market is now flooded with magazines, chiefly from the United States, which do not inculcate Canadian sentiment and nationality; and
Whereas the large amount of advertising matter in many of those magazines is detrimental to Canadian industry; and
Whereas this condition prevents the foundation of Canadian magazines, the growth of those which now exist, and thus restricts the market in Canada to the detriment of the interests of Canadian writers;
Be it resolved, that the Canadian-Authors Association go on record in favour of a duty to be levied on the advertising matter in magazines imported into Canada and this meeting directs that copies of this resolution be sent to the secretary of the Canadian National Newspapers and Periodicals Association, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and to the Minister of Finance.
Similar resolutions have been passed by the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Association of Canadian Clubs, and a great many other organizations. For example, the Brantford Chamber of Commerce has passed a very strong resolution. So, Sir, this question has been discussed in those circles which are interested in the permanence and prosperity of our periodical press.

Canadian Magazines
May I point out another thing? I think an examination of the facts will demonstrate that the great majority of the best writers of fiction in the English language began their work of authorship on the periodical press. Authors like Dickens, Thackeray, and others first had their productions published in the magazines of the day. The magazine press provides a vehicle for the development of literary talent, and no other medium so good can be found. It provides a means for the young man or young woman having literary talent to develop that talent under the very best conditions.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to make a constructive suggestion. Perhaps it has already been placed before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), but I would like to present it to the House. I would suggest that a tariff be put upon the advertising sections of American magazines. That is a perfectly logical proposal in view of the present tariff. If any one desires to circulate in this country printing matter for advertising purposes produced in the United States he must pay an import duty of fifteen cents a pound; if he is importing white paper he pays a duty of 25 per cent. Here are magazines of from 150 to 180 pages, of which probably more than three-quarters are advertising matter, but because there is a modicum of stories mixed up with these advertisements the latter are not subject to any tariff whatever. All that is necessary to give our Canadian magazine publishers a reasonable opportunity for "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" is that the tariff now applied to advertising matter when it comes in loose or in a solid book be applied to the advertising portions of these magazines.
The figures which I am about to quote illuminate the situation very much, although they cover only four publications. These figures, I may add, are prepared by the Canadian National Newspaper and Periodical Association. If a duty of fifteen cents per pound were placed on the advertising space in the Saturday Evening Post, the Ladies' Home Journal, the American Magazine and Good Housekeeping, it would amount altogether to $644,760 a year. The Saturday Evening Post would pay on each issue $7,540. And why should it not? It contains nearly two hundred pages, of which about one hundred and fifty are devoted entirely to the advertising of American goods-advertising space that our Canadian manufacturers cannot use at all- and comes into this country to the destruction of our magazine industry. The Ladies' Home Journal would pay over $16,000 odd on every
