issue because of the tremendous volume of its advertising. I submit that my proposal is a very fair one and I hope that the Minister of Finance will give it consideration when preparing his budget.
What postal rates do these magazines pay coming into Canada?

They come in largely by freight. But the Saturday Evening Post enjoys our postal privileges, and I think about a dozen other magazines as well. The Saturday Evening Post has no more right to our postal privileges than any other magazine published in the United States. Although it violates all the regulations of the Post Office Department, it gets those privileges. Undoubtedly it should not come in here under postal rates at all. However, I am not striking at one publication, I am trying rather to get at the principle involved. I would suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that he consider this question from the three or four standpoints I have tried to present: First, from the standpoint of the necessity of developing Canadian sentiment, the wisdom of providing some agency by which	the
aspirations of one part of Canada may be communicated to the other, and to try to make it possible by fair conditions for national publications to circulate all over Canada-throughout the Maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, the prairies and British Columbia. I believe there is enough enterprise and ability among Canadian business men to establish this industry if given a fair chance; but they have not got a fair chance under present conditions.
I would like my hon. friend to consider the question, too, from the standpoint of the manufacturers. I am not speaking for them alone, but when the enterprise of a Canadian manufacturer becomes successful it means a great deal for the men employed, for no manufacturer can succeed without hundreds, and in some cases thousands, of our men, being able to earn good wages and to maintain happy homes. In the interests of the men who are employed in those industries I would ask the Minister of Finance to consider the imposition of such a duty as I have suggested. In view of the fact that the great volume of these American magazines entering Canada consists of advertising matter, I hope my hon. friend will deal with it as he would deal with any other matter entering Canada for advertising purposes.

I understand that a good many of these trashy magazines contain very little

Canadian Magazines

advertising. How would my hon. friend's suggestion meet the case these present?

My hon. friend has heard the Minister of Customs tell us that he has banned some of these magazines. I think that is the proper way to deal with meretricious or suggestive stuff. It has been proposed' in some quarters that instead of a tax on advertising matter there should be a tax of ten cents a pound on the whole magazine. I would be quite as willing to accept that a_s the other, but of course.it is for the government to decide whether or not a tariff duty should be imposed, and if so, what form it should take. But if it is desirable to keep out the class of magazine the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) refers to, then a tax of ten cents a pound oil the whole magazine would be the proper way to deal with the matter.

I do not intend to say anything in regard to the financial points that have been brought up by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), but I would point out that there is need for exercising care in the matter of banning literature from the country. We all agree that literature which is obscene or low in its tendency should be banned; I believe the law already covers that. But the hon. gentleman read a resolution that had been sent to him or obtained by him from some Liberal association of Toronto, and I was verw sorry to notice in that resolution the word "censor" was used. If I remember rightly, the question of censoring literature was dealt with some two hundred years ago or more by John Milton in his Speech for the Liberty of unlicensed Printing; if hon. members will read that they will find the question fairly well dealt with.
There are a number of things that I believe should be kept out of the country, but we must be very careful before we put any hindrance upon the free entrance of books; he will need to be an able person who makes a decision in respect to which the life or death of a book is at stake. The danger of attempting to shut out magazines is that in keeping out the poor ones you may keep out also the good ones, in attempting to eliminate the tares you may at the same time destroy the wheat. I doubt whether the adoption of the procedure advocated by the hon. gentleman would ever produce a Canadian literature. We cannot produce a Canadian literature simply by taking steps to provide cheap paper, or by imposing a duty on magazines or anything of that kind.

The hon. member spoke about the magazines failing, about their ceasing publication. The question arises, why? The people buy certain magazines, and I believe that if we had the kind of magazine we should have, it would be bought, and the question would not be asked whether it was Canadian or American. In other words, if we deliver the goods we shall be able to get the price. If these magazines have failed, it is because, as the hon. member said, some of them started a puzzle department or adopted a plan of giving away an automobile for every new subscriber, and so on. That would put any magazine out of business.
I wish to quote from an article I read in the paper the other day in which reference is made to an address delivered in this city by Sir Henry Newbolt. It says:
"You do not build a great literature like a building of brick and stone that can be bought with money; you can only get it when a nation cannot rest satisfied until it does secure it," Sir Henry Newbolt is reported to have said in his lecture in Ottawa. In this pronouncement, there is a challenge both to Canadian readers and to Canadian writers. Is the nation displaying any restlessness in the interests of a great literature?
I wish to call the hon. gentleman's attention to that question. Does he find any universal demand for a Canadian literature?
Not sufficient to interrupt the stream of normal life. But the public is not indifferent. It is reading more to-day, and better. Yet it refuses to buy Canadian literature if better literature comes from outside, and in every department of letters, with one or two special exceptions, better literature is coming from outside.
That, I think, is from an Ottawa newspaper.

Is the hon. gentleman not aware that many of the best Canadian writers, because of the lack of a market for their product here-the lack of any channel for its distribution-went to the United States, contributed to United States magazines and became American citizens, and that that literature now comes to us through those American sources?

Certainly, I am well aware of that. I am aware also that some of them have gone to England-Sir Gilbert Parker, for instance. We can name a number of our writers who have gone to England and who have contributed to English magazines. But as I understand it, Mr. Speaker, the question is, can we produce a great Canadian literature by banning other literature? Is that the way it has ever been done before? Go back to the ways of Shakespeare and Milton and other great English writers; did their contributions to literature come about by the shutting out of literary works from other

Canadian Magazines
countries? Shall we ever become a literary people simply by keeping out of our country the magazines, and so on, that might be an example to us in our writing? The mere fact that our writers had to go to the United States and to England would indicate that they were able to get their articles published in a better class of magazine. If we produce a better magazine in Canada it will be purchased in Canada and read in Canada; then we shall have an important medium for the publication of articles written by our own writers. I do not believe a Canadian literature can be created by taxing the advertising in certain magazines. I do not believe we can bring about the publication of good Canadian magazines simply by shutting out those from other countries. What we have to do is to encourage the reading of good literature; that is the best way to induce good writing. I do not believe we have in Canada to-day what may be called a Canadian literature pure and simple. We have to create a demand for good books. Why is so much of this cheap stuff from the United States sold in Canada? Because there is a demand for it. Are we to create a demand for something better simply by shutting that out? It cannot be done in that way. We heard our friends the Progressives lectured the other day for introducing moral measures, for trying to put us in a good moral position.
I merely wish to enter a protest against the taking of any action that would prevent reading matter that would be of benefit to our people, from entering our country, I care not where it comes from. Moreover, I am afraid that when you introduce the thin end of the wedge, when you give authority to certain men to decide what magazines shall come in and what shall not, you are putting a power in their hands that they should not possess.

I may point out to my hon. friend that I did not propose banning any newspaper. I did not propose to tax any reading matter; I did not propose to keep it out. I proposed simply that the tariff now on advertising matter should be applied to the advertising matter in magazines.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in
agreement with the mover of the resolution, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), in regard to the questionable character of a great many of the American magazines that come into Canada, and I was very much pleased to hear the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) make the statement that he was banning certain of these magazines.
53J
I have very great respect for the views of the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Robinson), but I believe we should ban a great many of the publications that are at present coming into this country from the United States. However, I do not find myself in such general agreement with my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) as to the remedy. In fact, I would take the opposite course, and in that respect I am very pleased to find that I have been able to convert the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) to my view as to part of the remedy at least. Instead of putting a duty on the magazines coming in I would take the duty off the print paper coming in. It is hot that to which I hope to convert the hon. leader of the Opposition at the present time, but I was very much interested to hear him state in a previous debate this afternoon that he would like to see the exportation of pulpwood prohibited, or a large export duty put on it. That is what I have advocated every session since I have been in this House, and I remember very well that when I proposed it two years ago the present leader of the Opposition, who was then leading the government, had quite a good laugh at my expense. I am pleased, however, to observe that I am converting him to my view.

Is that a good free trade
measure?
That is why I laughed.

I think it would help
to remedy the present situation with regard to Canadian magazines. The publisher of one of the best Canadian magazines told me less than two weeks ago that he could buy his paper in the United States, pay the duty on it and the extra cent-and-a-half sales tax on the imported article, and still get his paper cheaper than he could buy it in Canada.
What kind of paper was it?

Magazine
paper, I suppose.

The same quality of paper he would buy in Canada. That was the statement he made. While for a time to prohibit the exportation of pulpwood would work a seeming hardship on our producers of pulpwood, really it would have a healthy effect on the manufacture of paper in this country. We have practically a monopoly of the spruce wood of North America, and the United States must have our pulp. If they cannot get the raw pulp they are getting now free of duty they would establish pulp and

Canadian Magazines
paper mills in Canada, and it would mean the development of possibly one of the largest industries Canada could hope to secure.
They are doing that right along.

I would like to show what is happening to our natural resources, in view of the discussion we have had this afternoon as to the depletion of our forests. I have here a prospectus issued by the Oxford Paper Company of Rumford Falls, Maine, dated June 1, 1922.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'cock, I was endeavouring to show some reasons why the Canadian publishers cannot compete with the American publishers in the publication of magazines, and in order to do this I wish to quote from a prospectus issued by the Oxford Paper Company, Rumford, Maine, in June 1922. They were issuing this prospectus for the purpose of selling $3,000,000 worth of stock to develop the pulp and paper industry in the United States, and I want to give the House what they quoted as the large or important part of their assets. The prospectus starts out with this statement:
The company has been a successful manufacturer of paper for more than twenty years. It owns and operates large plants at Rumford, Maine, manufacturing book paper, coated paper, soda pulp, sulphite pulp and electrolytic bleach. It also owns all the capital stock of Rumford Falls Power Company, which owns and operates the entire electric and hydraulic development at Rumford, including a modem hydro-electric plant with a present installed capacity of 31,000 horse power. An ample supply of electric power and water for the company's present and future needs is thus assured. It also controls a large acreage of spruce and fir timber at various places in Canada, sufficient for 100 years' supply at the company's present rate of consumption.
It enumerates the different holdings which they have in Canada and says:
The company's available supply of pulpwood is ample. It holds under lease from the Crown the right to cut and remove pulpwood and all forest growth from a tract of about 1,015 square miles (approximately 650,000 acres) in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. This lease runs for a long term of years in twenty year renewable period, the last maturing June 19, 1998, at an annual rental of $6,000. This rental is a fixed sum, regardless of the amount of wood cut from these lands. These holdings are virgin forests and contain, according to conservative estimates by experts, at least 6,000,000 cords of high grade pulpwood sufficient to supply Oxford Paper Company for more than 100 years at its present rate of consumption of spruce and fir.

In addition, the company owns the right for 12 years to cut spruce and fir from a track of 55,000 acres in Canada, near the city of Quebec, and also has the right to cut spruce and fir from 125,000 acres additional Crown lands in Canada.
The company has a further large available supply of spruce and fir and pulp through its one-half ownership of Nashwaak Pulp and Paper Company, Limited, which owns in New Brunswick a pulp mill and owns or controls about 359,000 acres of land containing about 1,000,000 cords of spruce and fir timber.
This is the reason I say that I believe the federal government, if they do not prohibit the exportation of pulpwood entirely, should at least put a very high export duty on it. Before the House rose at six o'clock when I suggested this export duty or prohibition of exports, I think I heard the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) make the remark that it was immoral. Well, Mr. Speaker, if it is immoral to conserve the supply of raw material in Canada for one of the most important industries in Canada, to say nothing ,of the vast importance of the forest growth of this country, in order to protect even plant life in Canada, it is certainly more immoral to allow that raw material to go out free and then to charge a 25 per cent duty on the finished product when it is imported.
I do not want to be misquoted. I said I considered the principle of an export duty as immoral, and I do.

I am pleased that I did not misquote the hon. member, and I still contend that if it is immoral to conserve our natural products in Canada by any method we see fit, it is much more immoral to allow them to go out of the country free, and then charge a high import duty on the finished article which our people must buy. I said that I found myself in general agreement with the mover of this resolution as to the quality of the publications coming into this country from the United States, but I find myself at very great variance with him as to the remedy. My remedy would be to remove the duty, not only from the paper which enters into Canadian magazines, but from the printer's ink, printer's type, if they are not already exempt, and every other item of tariff that enters into the expense of making Canadian magazines. It is very important that we should have Canadian magazines. I do not wish to cover all the ground covered by the mover of the resolution; he did it much better than I could. I think we will all agree with him that American magazines which come into this country, not only contain literature of a very low type which tends to lower the morals of our people, but, as he so well put it, advertise American products, boost the United States as a country and, I think, are

Canadian Magazines
a large factor in inducing our young people to migrate to the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself very largely in agreement with the sentiment contained in this resolution, but I am not in agreement with the proposed remedy. Anything which tends to create a national feeling is very much to be desired, but it takes more than sentiment to create national unity. The mover of this resolution (Mr. Hocken) wants, I believe, a duty of some 10 cents per pound placed on Canadian magazines. My opinion is that we have too much protection of this kind already in this country on everything. If we want national unity, this whole country must be put on an equal basis as regards opportunity. Many Canadian magazines and periodicals that are now facing ruin, if that be true-and I believe to some extent it is-or who find it hard to live and prosper-have advocated protection so much that their own pyramid is at last tumbling down on their heads. The protection they have so long advocated has at last made the cost of living and the cost of production so much out of line, so high, that their productions are altogether out of line as to cost with that of those with whom they have to compete.
It is said that nearly 2,500,000 pounds of United States' magazines were carried a year ago by the Canadian mails, and that fact is used by magazine publishers as an argument for more protection. To me, it conveys the fact that there is in Canada a wide reading public, and did we follow a just economic system, that 2,500,000 pounds could be very largely supplied by our own countrymen. Only to-day I received a letter from the Canadian National Newspaper and Periodical Association in which they state that Canadian magazine publishers have to pay from 25 to 40 per cent more for their material than United States publishers, and this, in spite of the fact that a very large percentage of pulp used in the manufacture of book paper in the United States is the product of Canadian forests. So, we are in this country at this time in the position of supplying the United States with the material from our natural resources and paying duty on the finished article from that product. The magazine publishers' association really admit the fact that they are paying from 25 to 40 per cent more for the material because of this trade penalty which we have placed on that product. Were it not for this, it seems to me that they would be well able to compete against all comers.
Senator Willis, of Ohio, is reported by the New York Herald to have stated at a recent
dinner of the American Paper and Pulp Association that Canada can produce mechanical pulp 23 per cent lower and chemical pulp 19 per cent lower than these can be produced in the United States. Why, then, should Canadian publishers have to pay from 25 to 40 per cent higher prices for their supplies of book and half-tone paper? We are in the position of having the raw material; but owing to this short-sighted policy of trade restriction by a protective tariff, we have driven the cost of production so high that we cannot make the use we should of our own natural resources. The Woman's Century and the Canadian Courier were forced out of existence by high production costs, with very heavy loss, I believe, in one case. I would be in favour of giving these people relief by the removal of the duty altogether from book print, and I would move that this motion be amended by adding thereto the following words:
placing on the free list all material used in the production of Canadian magazines and newspapers.
Mr. JOHN A. MacKELVIE (Yale): Mr. Speaker, I find myself very heartily in accord with every word advanced by the mover of this resolution (Mr. Hocken); nor, since he took his seat, have I heard from other members who have spoken on the subject anything that has changed my viewpoint in the slightest. An hon. member across the way objected strongly to the idea of censorship of any kind, calling in support of his contention the somewhat celebrated pamphlet by Milton on the freedom of the press. I do not know that that is particularly germane to the subject under dischssion, but something can be said for censorship. It may be remembered that not many years following the utterance of Milton, a vast revulsion took place in England at the time of the Restoration, and the literature of that age which found expression through the drama, while sparkling in many instances with wit and humour, was so lewd in its nature as to lead up before many years to a strict censorship which barred it from the stage. I suppose most of us in this House have reached such years and, I hope, such maturity of judgment, as not to be particularly affected by reading such things. Many of us probably have enjoyed the wit of Congreve, Fletcher, Marlowe and other dramatists; but we would not care to place them for indiscriminate distribution amongst the young people of the land. Those of us who can take enjoyment in Boccaccio would not care to hanfl over the Decameron to the school boys and girls of the country. So something can, after all, be said for censorship which
Canadiar, Magazines

we also cany on in a very sensible manner in conection with our moving picture shows.
But the argument advanced by the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) presents a new phase of the question. I do not suppose that it is necessary, for me to inform the members of this House that I am a firm believer in the policy of protection as applied to our industries; and here I find myself more consistent in the support of such views than the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) can claim for his position. While he has frequently enlightened the House as to his ideas regarding trade, and has fulminated against anything in the way of restriction in this country, now that he finds himself particularly interested in an industry that is of great importance to the district from which *he comes, he is quite willing to throw aside his principles and advocate that an export- duty be placed on pulpwood. It all depends on whose ox is gored; that is the attitude of a great many hon. gentlemen in this House.
Referring, however, to the resolution moved by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), I think he so admirably covered all the ground that it is hardly necessary for me to enlarge on any of his arguments. But I may remark that if ever there was a time in the history of our national life when it was important that some factor should be encouraged and cherished which would have the effect of bringing about a unification of Canadian sentiment and of making conditions better known to our people both east and west, that time is the present. And I think no more important factor could call for support than that of developing to as large an extent as possible a real Canadian literature embodied in weekly or monthly publications.
The remedy suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) is that in order to give protection to this industry another industry which was built up at the expenditure of a great deal of capital in Canada should be sacrificed. He would remove the duty from paper irrespective of the damage which that would do to our paper mills in this country, giving no consideration to the numbers who would thereby be thrown out of employment, and regardless of the death blow such an action would bring to a rapidly growing and very important business. But the remedy which he proposes does not in fact secure the relief which those seek who are supporting the resolution. It is rather astonishing that members outside a particular line of business, who cannot be expected to have

any technical knowledge of that business, should suggest some remedy which those who are personally interested in the business are sure would be of no effect. It is not a reduction in the duty on paper that is asked for by the resolution. If the supporters of the resolution needed that form of relief they would no doubt request it. On the contrary, they have a specific remedy which they desire to advance in behalf of their position, and that remedy has been well set forth in the resolution.
Now, Sir, I do not intend to speak at any length on the subject, but I cannot help observing that there was some force in one of the arguments submitted by the mover of the resolution in regard to the question of emigration from Canada. We have heard a good deal about immigration this session, and I expect we shall hear a great deal more befor'e the session closes. In this connection I would read a brief extract from an article which appeared recently in the Financial Post bearing on this subject.
Westerners are beginning to worry about the effect that articles in United * States magazines are having upon Canadian emigration. In western Canada where crops and prices are temporarily unsatisfactory and have created some discontent, the articles in these United States publications play up incessantly and inaccurately the doings of Americans and the attractions of United States life. The natural result is that readers want to go where they think life is more enjoyable and they are going in thousands. Many of them are native born Canadians and Old Country people. Letters show they are not finding the happiness they expected.
The rosy picture placed before the readers of scores of these magazines has had its effect in this direction, I have no doubt; and it is rather a hopeless situation in which Canadian publications find themselves. Glancing through nearly every month a number of these American publications, I find in some of the best of them much to interest and amuse me and, occasionally, some information that is not easily accessible in any other form. But I will say that except as regards those of the very highest type, the average publication from the other side which is displayed on the news stands of this country does not at all compare in literary merit to the average Canadian publication. I am convinced that given a fair show and a free field, and allowed to develop as it should, it would not be long before a real Canadian literature could be built up. As pointed out by the mover of the resolution, there is no method better calculated to develop and foster a literature than serial publications in magazine form. That has been found to be the case in other countries and it will be the case in Canada. I am convinced that the elimination from our

Canadian Magazines
news stands and general circulation of a lot of the more trashy publications which are sold in such large quantities, and the substitution therefor of Canadian magazines of the type we now have, would be of inestimable benefit to the citizens of Canada. The cheaper magazines of American publication are incomparably inferior to the best of ours and will not average up even to the lowest standard of publication we produce in this country. I am not dwelling on the salacious aspects of the literature provided by many of those publications, because I admit that a great many of them are tolerably free from that imputation. Some of them, however, which are among the most widely circulated and pretentious of American magazines are full of literature of a very, insidious and debasing type. I have great pleasure in supporting the resolution.

I have a great deal of sympathy with the majority of statements which have been made during this debate this afternoon and evening. I can very well understand that it is desirable that we should have a Canadian literature. But it is a far greater problem to say how we are going to get the Canadian people to read it. I think it would be a mistake to place a ban on any literature that is coming to this country, because the moment you do so you shut out to that extent the light from the people who desire it. It may be that the great mass of the Canadian people have not been prepared to receive the literature that we as a people would like them to read. But even if the supposed remedy were placed on the statute books, whereby we placed ten cents of a duty on every magazine coming into Canada from the United States, if the Canadian people wanted that magazine they would pay that extra ten cents. In other words, they would get it in spite of anything we might do in the way of taxation.
I fully appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that our literature is of great educational value, and that the kind of literature we read will to a large extent mould our public life. For that reason I would be very glad if our people would read Canadian literature. But at the present time many American magazines have a large circulation in this country, and the greater proportion of them are of value to our people. I do not need to mention any particular magazine, but I do not think it will be disputed that some of these American magazines are almost indispensable to us at the present time. Whether we in Canada, even if we had the opportunity, would be able to produce such magazines is open to question.
I have looked at this problem from a good many standpoints, and if the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) is in order I shall support it, because I do believe it is a step in the right direction. I do not altogether agree with the argument advanced by the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. MacKelvie) that it would be a death blow to other industries if the tariff were removed from the materials that enter into the manufacture of Canadian magazines, because they are produced from our own natural resources. It does seem to me that our manufacturers of pulp and paper, having their raw materials right at hand, should be able to compete with our American friends who have to buy their raw material from us. For that reason I think the argument of the hon. member for Saskatoon is well founded.
I do not altogether agree with the criticism directed against the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) by the last speaker, namely, that he was inconsistent in advocating an export duty to preserve our Canadian forests. It does seem to me, whether we be free trade people or not, when we find Canadian business men devastating our natural resources and despoiling our forests for the sake of gain, and thus denying to posterity its rights that the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton was taking a fair view of the situation in advocating an export duty on pulpwood. Such a duty would at least be killing two birds with the one stone: it would assist our revenue on the one hand, and on the other hand it would also help to preserve this national resource.
Now, I can hardly see the connection between emigration and foreign literature. It must be admitted that although American magazines colour our national life to a large extent, yet we derive certain advantages from their perusal. But that reading matter in the shape of Snappy Stories has such a decisive influence upon the lives of some of our people as to impel them to cross over to the American side is more than I am willing to admit. The only reason why people emigrate to another country is that economic conditions practically force them to go where they can make a good living. Therefore I do not believe that merely by imposing a tariff upon American magazines we shall be able to stop the flow of emigration from this country to the United States.
I would like to see Canadian publishers build up a large magazine industry that would offset the sale of American magazines in this country. But we cannot ignore the grave disadvantage which they are labouring under at
Canadian Magazines

the present time. At best they must find their circulation among a population of only nine million, and this limited output renders it impossible for them to pay the high prices for articles and stories that American publishers offer to successful authors. As a result we find that many Canadian authors go to the United States, attracted by the higher remuneration which they can command there. To a large extent we benefit by getting better magazines from the American side. Of course, on the other hand, there is a great deal of trash coming into this country from the United States, much of morbid suggestiveness. But at the same time many people in Canada delight in that kind of reading. Why, it is sold on our trains. You cannot go on a railway journey without a news agent coming along and putting the latest number of Spicy Stories in your hand. And I admit that sometimes after a hard day's work in parliament or somewhere else, when you are tired and weary, a spicy story is all right.
Oh, oh.

I am speaking out quite
frankly.
Hear, hear.

But I do not believe the reading of this trash is good for our youth. When ' we consider the cosmopolitan character of some parts of our population, people not even with British or French traditions, the circulation of these trashy magazines is not conducive to inculcating in them ideals of Canadian citizenship. Consequently I was delighted this afternoon to hear that the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) is willing to ban any reading matter that drops too low in the moral scale.
I hope that if this House sees fit to adopt the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), it will put our Canadian publishers on the right road to success, and I trust that our great educationalists and others who have the benefit of the public at heart will see to it that in our schools, our collegiates and our universities our youth are trained to read good literature. We cannot legislate our young men and women to read the classics, but we can train them in the home and so mould their literary taste that they will be able to sift the chaff from the wheat and read the solid achievements of literature. It is only by cultivating a taste for good reading and building up a Canadian literature that the people of Canada will themselves be able to discriminate between what is good and what is worthless in litera-
TMr. Lewis.]
ture and select what they feel is best suited to nurture Canadian ideals.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself in a general way with the resolution of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). I fear the discussion this afternoon has wandered a good deal from the resolution, and therefore I shall ask the House to consider its exact terms.
That, in tho opinion of this House, it is desirable that measures should be adopted to encourage the publication of Canadian magazines and periodicals.
That resolution, it seems to me, should appeal to every member of this House, irrespective of party or creed. I regret-and I say this quite sincerely-that more hon. gentlemen representing the province of Quebec have not supported it. There is a very fine French Canadian literature of which the French Canadian people are naturally very proud, and I must say I had expected to see a number of hon. gentlemen from Quebec very quickly support the resolution. I regret also that hon. members to my left have made it a question of tariff. I do not think that the tariff enters very much into it. The main objection raised by the publishers of this country is that the American periodicals, being supported by a much larger population, are more attractive, probably, so far as general appearance goes; that they have a larger circulation and consequently a larger income, and on the whole can turn out a more attractive publication, and that they, are pushing out of the market in Canada the admirable Canadian magazines of which we have quite a number. That would appear to be the general opinion of the publishers as set forth in the literature which they have sent to hon. members of the House.
I agree with other speakers that to ban literature is, generally speaking, not the best way to keep it out of the country, though it may succeed to a certain extent. I remember well travelling in Germany on one occasion and almost everywhere on the doors of cars over the entrance to buildings, and so on, the word "verboten" appeared. They were "verboten" to do this and "verboten" to do that, until one got very tired of looking al that German word. I do not think we should in this country follow that line of thought. I am not one of those who believe that we can legislate ourselves into heaven, or legislate the people of this country into heaven. Probably we would have a better chance to succeed hereafter if we faced at least some of the trials which beset us rather than attempt to wipe them all out. I do not think

Canadian Magazines
you can strengthen a child's back, for example, by putting a corset on it from its babyhood; and that is what is too often attempted in legislation. So that I do not believe in banning literature, generally speaking, though I have no quarrel with what has already been done in that respect; some of the literature excluded was spicy, to use the expression of my hon. friend who preceded me (Mr. Lewis), and might well be refused admission to this country. 1 noticed that Victor Margueritte o! France, was the other day expelled from the Legion of Honour for writing a book which was a little too spicy, and I understand that over a quarter of a million copies of the book in question have already been sold in France ; so that it is usually one of the best methods of advertising literature to say that it should not be read. There is enough of old Adam in practically every member of this House-possibly with some exceptions-to induce him to read any of these books. I am sure that if the Library should get a copy of Marguerittes's "La Gar?onne," the rush on the part of hon. members to read it would be so great that it would be necessary to have duplicate copies.
It has been pointed .out here to-day that the value of the American periodicals coming into this country in 1922 was something like $3,000,000. That is quite an importation, particularly when we are endeavouring, or should be endeavouring, to lessen our importations from the United States, if from no other reason than that we would prefer to have our exchange on a basis of par. The following are the six magazines having the highest circulation of the American magazines which come here. They are not given in their order, but these are the pre-eminent ones:	Pictorial
Review, Cosmopolitan, Ladies' Home Journal, Red Book, Delineator, Saturday Evening Post. I should like to ask hon. members of this House this question: If through some catastrophe any or all of these six happened to fail to reach this country during the next year or so, would there be any real damage done to the people?
You could always read the Orange Sentinel.
I always read it?
You could always read that instead.
My hon. friend himself always reads high class literature, so I am sure he would read the Orange Sentinel.
It is good literature, anyway.

I do not know that I could always agree with that to the same extent as I do with the resolution of my hon. friend. However, I did not get up to discuss the Orange Sentinel; it does not come into this resolution, I understand. I was going on to say that I myself enjoy reading these magazines on occasions, and I am sure many hon. members do the same thing. But if any of them, through some accident, failed to come here, I doubt whether there would be any permanent harm done to the people of this country. It is true there are very good magazines published in the United States, and if some measures are taken to keep out of this country or to limit the circulation here of American magazines, some exceptions could easily be worked out to permit magazines of the higher type to come in without difficulty.
I wish to offer four main grounds upon which I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) might give serious heed to the representations of the hon. member for West Toronto in this connection. In the first place, practically all the magazines that the hon. member for West Toronto is aiming at are luxuries. If, therefore, some extra tax were put upon them it would simply be a method of taxing luxuries. Even my hon. friends to my left, who interject free trade into all these questions that come up in the House- even they, I imagine, who know by now, or ought to know, unless they are much more dense than I think they are, that they are not going to get free trade-

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he is not aware that the Magazine Publishers' Association itself has made a tariff question out of this matter? One of the grievances they lay down is that all of the materials that go into and are used in the manufacture of Canadian periodicals are protected by a tariff resulting in the Canadian publisher paying from 25 to 40 per cent more for his raw materials than the United States publisher.

I am not trying to voice the opinions of the Canadian publishers; I am simply giving my own. But even so, that is only one of the reasons which the Canadian publishers give. I think they submit in their literature that the important reason why their magazines are not read as widely as they should be is that the American magazines have such a large circulation in this country. I was going on to say that even the veriest free trader among my hon. friends to my left would take the attitude of taxing luxuries, and the Minister of Finance, if he
Canadian Magazines

puts any tax upon these American periodicals, will be taxing luxuries.
Why?
Because they are luxuries.
Literature is a luxury?
Most of the literature of which we are speaking is entirely a luxury.
That is, the spicy part.

Some of it, I should say, is an injurious luxury. In the second place, my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, would be raising revenue. The figures given by the publishers' association show that the revenue resulting from a tax of 10 cents per pound on American magazines or of 15 cents per pound on advertising would result in a revenue of a million dollars or more-and I do not suppose there is anybody who knows better than the Minister of Finance that revenue is a very important thing. In the third place, it would aid Canadian literature, and I think it is the desire of every member of this House to do that if at all possible. Finally, it would help to build up a Canadian national spirit, something which I think we lack. Unfortunately, due to the immensity of our land, due to its various sections having different interests, our national spirit has not been developed as it should have been; to too great an extent we speak from the point of view of the sections that we represent. But this would appear to me to be one of the questions upon which we can speak as Canadian citizens without quarrelling from the standpoint of party or even of section, and we should endeavour to build up a greater Canadian national spirit in this country. All that is asked by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) and by the publishers is that some of the handicaps be removed. I do not care very much just how the Minister of Finance should happen to go about it, to put Canadian publications on the same level of marketability as the American publications. There is no doubt we have publications in this country, magazines which stand very high as reading matter. I will name only two of the best known; they are the Canadian Magazine and MacLean's, both of which have a pretty fair circulation in this country, and both of which furnish high-class reading matter.

The hon. member spoke of promoting French-Canadian literature and was surprised that nobody on this side spoke in favour of the resolution. In what way would the adoption of this resolution help

French-Canadian literature? Does my hon. friend think that the exclusion from this country of French literature or the imposition of a heavy tax on it would help French-Canadian literature?
The question gets us back to the sectionalism of which I spoke a moment ago.
Hear, hear.

Not at all. In what
way?

I do not say that this would distinctly aid French-Canadian literature, but if it would, that would be one more reason why the resolution should be adopted. The reason it may not help French-Canadian literature is that there is practically no French literature published in the United States. My hon. frend should be the first, and would be the first I am sure, to endeavour to build up Canadian literature even if it is not French-Canadian literature.

Hear, hear. But my hon. friend spoke of French-Canadian literature being built up through this resolution and expressed surprise that we were not supporting it. I simply asked how it was going to help French-Canadian literature.

I might point out to my hon. friend that there are a number of French Canadians who fairly often contribute to the English-speaking literature of this country, and in that way it would help French-Canadian literature.
French-Canadian literature in English.
My hon. friend should have no objection to that.
No, but that would be Canadian literature, not French-Canadian literature.

I hope my hon. friend always makes it straight Canadian literature, and straight Canadian questions when he discusses them throughout the country. When I mentioned French-Canadian literature I certainly did not mean to offend my hon. friend, but simply to take the attitude of boosting the French-Canadians as well as the other Canadians in this country. My hon. friend will agree with me that to a French-Canadian, Canadian means French-Canadian, and the others are English-Can-adians. I have read something of the people of Quebec and I know something of them.

Canadian Magazines

I am quite willing to
accept my friend as a Canadian.

Well, I am quite willing to accept my hon. friend as a Canadian also, so far as that goes. I do not think either one of us deserves any credit for accepting the other as such. Mr. Speaker, I did not mean to enter into any controversy with my hon. friend. I wish to say in closing that I think the Minister of Finance will be doing a favour to the people of this country, will be doing a favour not only to Canadian literature, but also to Canadian literature of the province of Quebec, if I may change my phraseology, by doing something to foster the building up of the literature which we have in this country to-day by endeavouring to implement the resolution proposed.

As an old newspaper man I may be allowed to say a few words on this subject. I am old enough to remember when the newspapers published in Canada had not been converted into omnibuses for the carrying of advertising. The old-time newspaper, which was a very small publication in its way, contained some editorials, a little news, and very little advertising. The difficulty with the modern newspaper of to-day is that it is so bulky and, to many readers so uninteresting. I have been ashamed of myself often in the railway stations at Montreal and elsewhere to see these huge masses of American newspapers coming into the country and flooding the English provinces more especially, for the reason that they are English publications-we are not threatened very much in that respect in the province of Quebec, except in the cities-and I have wondered whether it was because we had nothing worth reading in Canada or because American publication's contained a kind of literature which was not produced here.
In the United States, as elsewhere, there are many things worthy of the country in the way of books, magazines and newspapers of the highest order. It is so in England, in France and in Canada, but I am prepared to say, Mr. Speaker, that there are publications in the United States which should never be allowed into Canada. Whether this is a matter for the customs, for the post office or for the Minister of Finance, certainly some of these publications should be barred from the country if for no other reason than the moral reason and because they are antiCanadian and anti-British. We boast in the province of Quebec, and I know it is not an idle dream, to be very British, British to the core. We and those who came before us have proved it, and are ready to prove it again.
Glancing over the Hansard of some years ago I notice that when you,' Mr. Speaker, had the honour of being Postmaster General you gave the British magazines a preference in this country to offset this flood of American publications, and I notice that from 1908 to 1912, to judge by poundage only, according to post office regulations, the number of British publications coming to Canada had increased from 2,000,000 pounds to 5,500,000 pounds. This was a great advantage to the Britisher coming to Canada because he was able to get his own publications, his home newspaper and his home magazines out here, and it was brought about through what the Liberal party had done some years before in bringing about the penny postage. That stands to-day to the credit of the eminent Postmaster General who was successful in that undertaking. It is unfortunate, for some reason or other that I am not prepared to discuss now, that arrangement fell through. Sir George Foster in the course of the debate claimed that this arrangement with the British post office was not continued because the British post office did not carry its share of the burden, that the rate of postage had been reduced from eight to two cents a pound in England, and that Canada carried the whole cost across the ocean. At all events the arrangement fell through, and that is why not such 51 large number of British publications are read in Canada to-day as was the case then. I hope if such an arrangement can be revived at any time by the Postmaster General, that it will be done, because if I judge the sentiments of the Canadian people we intend to remain British in this country. We intend to make of Canada the leading nation in the Empire if we can do so, and for that reason we want to seek our information at the fountain source and to get from England-I mention England, but the arrangement would also be extended to France of course-publications which are hardly equalled and most certainly are not surpassed by anything in the United States of America.
We have every reason to remain on friendly terms with the United States. Our lot has been cast alongside theirs, and we will continue to be on friendly terms, I hope, as long as we continue to exist as a separate nation, and that I hope will be for many years to come. But I think the Minister of Finance would be well advised-and it is fortunate that in this present case the Minister of Finance is a veteran newspaper man who is in a position to judge of the situation,-to avail himself of any means of increasing the revenue of Canada through the mass of American literature which comes in here
Canadian Magazines

in the shape of newspapers, magazines or otherwise.
These are not essential to the Canadian reading public. I am not in favour of buying the literature of any country if it is obscene, or immoral, or contrary to public policy. But when I pick up a magazine with 20 or 30 pages of reading matter and 50 or 60 pages of advertising-which advertising is used in a way detrimental to the manufacturers and business men of this country-I do not see why Canada should not obtain some revenue out of the advertising. When we are taxed to the limit to-day, in all classes of society, federally, provincially and municipally, we should find some means of increasing our revenue by taxing in some shape or form this method of advertising American goods in Canada through the medium of American newspapers or American magazines.
I am speaking more especially of the city of Montreal at pre^nt. We have now in Montreal English and French newspapers, well illustrated, issued on Saturday, which compare very favourably with the publications brought in from the United States. The advantage of circulation of the Canadian newspapers is that they assist in creating a national spirit, and we are all prepared to admit that if Canada is to continue to live it must be united. Canadians must come to understand each other better and cease to be divided by provincial lines. Those who came before us may have divided this country for the purpose of administration on provincial lines,' but surely the day is not far distant when a Canadian will realize that the whole of Canada is his country and that he is not peculiarly a citizen of any one province. This national spirit can best be created, fostered and encouraged by publications in Canada which are filled with Canadian ideas and Canadian ideals, and its interests can be built up by circulation of its own as well as by publications from the Mother Country. In this country the Canadians have the advantage of two mother lands. We have what is called the Mother Land and also what has been called our stepmother land. However, from the literature of France and from the literature of England, Scotland and Ireland, Canadians can draw from abroad all the inspiration that is necessary. We must build up Canadian sentiment. The most powerful instrument to-day in modern times is no doubt the newspaper press. The newspaper to-day is the most powerful instrument in civilization for good or for evil.
If a way can be found of preventing the flooding of this country by that which is not

helpful, by that which is damaging to it, by that which is permeating the whole body politic of Canada and creating imperceptibly in the younger and rising generation ideas which we should not encourage, I hope the veteran Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), will find it, with the assistance of the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy). Whatever change is brought about, not simply the means proposed in the amendment of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans), but by all other means, either through the post office regulations, or by some variation of the tariff, I know that the Minister of Finance will feel it his duty to encourage the effort that is now being made to give to the Canadian people the intellectual food so necessary in the formation of a virile national sentiment, and nothing, I consider, is more important to the people than the newspaper they read day by day. It was said by an old philosopher in olden times, and I think the Minister of Finance repeated the quotation some few days ago-
I care not who makes the laws of the country, if I but write its songs.
If you can succeed in placing in every Canadian home a Canadian newspaper, bound up with with Canadian ideals, striving through its every effort to make Canada what we want Canada to become, you will be giving that house and that family the most valuable of all assistance. Some years ago there was published in the city of Montreal-and it is still published under another name-a newspaper called the Montreal Witness. We did not always share its views, but it was an honest paper, and whenever one entered the house where the Witness was to be seen we knew what the sentiments of that family were. I wish it were the case now with every newspaper and periodical published in Canada. But surely", as between the two, there should be no hesitation, and I know that if the Minister of Finance can do so he will try, in a friendly way and not in a hostile spirit, wherever an American publication appears, to give an equal chance to a Canadian publication, and if he succeeds the benefit to this country will be very great.

I should like to support the amendment of .the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans). It seems to be the only way of accomplishing the end which the resolution calls for. As for the resolution itself, while I will be very heartily in favour of it in the form in which it stands as an encouragement to the publication of Canadian magazines and the development of Canadian literature, I

Canadian Magazines
would hesitate to vote for it because of the interpretation which has been placed on it by the mover (Mr. Hocken) and those who have supported it. If a vote in favour of this resolution simply means that we are going to place a sort of a duty on magazines coming in from outside, it seems to me we are moving in the wrong direction. It is all very well, perhaps, for us to object to certain classes of American magazines. We have some literature that is below par in the United States and we mast confess that we have some literature in Canada that is below par. There is certain literature that does not tend to foster a unified Canadian life. I think we all agree that we want to develop in this country that literature that does foster unity. We want to do everything in our power to develop a high type Canadian literature, but you cannot do that simply by putting a ban, or an embargo or a duty, upon literature coming from other countries.
We heard some strong words here the other day directed against paternalism. I wonder if we are going to submit to the paternalism that will indicate to us just what we should read.
I am rather surprised that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) should seek to enact a new sort of Index Expurgatorius-a Canadian Index-that will decide for the Canadian people exactly what type of literature they should read. It would seem rather as if, instead of banning ideals from the other side of the line, we should welcome them, yes, welcome ideals from whatever source they may come. We must recognize that just south of the line there is a great population of over
100,000,000 people, people speaking the same language that we do, people who have a much longer history than the English speaking peoples of Canada, people who have had time to develop a very considerable literature, people who have a certain class that is more or less free to do writing, people who have the same old English backgrounds, and to a large extent the same British institutions that we have in Canada, people who to a considerable degree have the same social ideals that we have and, I would say, people with whom, whether we like this or not, the future of Canada at least socially is inevitably bound up. With these hundred million people to the south of us, we must surely look for a development of literature that is well worth while. Presumably from a hundred million people, there are likely to come more writers than from eight or nine million people. Presumably from a hundred million people there are likely to come men who will give us ideals that are
not simply the commercial ideals of which we are afraid, but ideals along all lines which we might well welcome in this country and use to our advantage. Think of the long list of high class, worth-while magazines which are now being published in the United States and which we could ill afford to do without. Why should these be put beyond the reach of the poorer people of this country? If we are to ban literature because it comes from the United States or some other place outside of Canada, shall we then proceed to ban painting or art or music that comes from outside of Canada? I should like to protest against a narrow parochialism that has more or less developed in this country. Rather, if we are going to build dp a unified Canadian sentiment and make life worth while in this country, we ought to welcome the highest and best in literature, art and music that comes to us from the United States and from all parts of Europe.
Mention has been made of our immigrant people. This thing I know, that if we are going to unite all our immigrant people into a new Canadian type, we shall have to be more hospitable to new ideals and ideas than we have been in the past.
I submit that the only practical solution has been put forward by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans). We cannot put an embargo on ideas; we cannot by taxation stimulate ideas or literature. The most we can do is to make it possible for men to express themselves, to cut down the cost incident to men expressing themselves. I would vote heartily for the resolution, if it meant that this House was extending in some other way by some other method an interest in Canadian literature. I rather regret that we have interpreted the British North America Act a little too narrowly and that this Canadian parliament has had so little to do with Canadian educational affairs. I would rather like to think that this parliament might subsidize, if you will, the various provincial governments in making more adequate provision for education. We are told that two or three or four or five and, perhaps, in this province six per cent of our people get through the high schools. If the education of the people of Canada remains that of the public schools, perhaps, even that of the lower grades of the public schools, we cannot very well hope for an appreciation of the highest and best in literature. I trust that this House will pass nothing that will make it more difficult for people to obtain information from the United States or from any other part of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to take up much of the

Canadian Magazines

time of this House. All that I intended saying has been so well said by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) that I feel it almost needless for me to say any more. I could very well have supported this resolution. I had not the privilege of hearing the mover (Mr. Hocken) deliver his address to the House. I gathered, however, that it was the mover of the resolution who introduced the question of a tariff in connection with this matter. I would like to say only this-and I say it good naturedly-I do not see why members to the right of me love so much to lecture hon. members who sit in this part of the House.
We are only returning some of your own medicine.
I suppose they are doing it kindly for our good and perhaps we shall be benefited by it to some extent.
Ultimately.

Ultimately. I have no doubt we have some parochialism in this part of the House, but, perhaps, parochialism may also be found in other parts of the House. I am not saying this in an ill-natured manner, but many hon. members have a tendency to tell us what they think about us and what we ought to do on all kinds of subjects.
I had intended giving the quotation which the hon. member for Bonaventure gave a little while ago of the philosopher who said:
I care not who makes the laws of the country, if I but write its songs.
I well believe the truth of that saying, that the literature of a country has certainly a great deal to do with the life and welfare of the nation which reads that literature.
As regards press censorship and censoring newspapers and periodicals that come from the United States, I have very much doubt whether that can be done. It has always been very dangerous when any set of men have undertaken to say what a people should or should not read. I certainly agree with the sentiment that nothing anti-British or antiCanadian should be allowed to come into this country, if we can possibly prevent its coming, and anything that can be done in that direction would, I am sure, receive my hearty support.
One thing that struck me during this debate was the remark that has been made so often that Canada is such a small country,-a country with only 9,000,000 people,-that it cannot expect to have any great literature.
I wonder if those who make such statements

have taken into account the fact that the grandest literature that the world has yet known was written by the natives of small countries. England was a very small country as regards population when Shakespeare wrote his immortal plays. Dante was not a native of the Empire of Germany, but of a very small state; and I hope hon. members will not think I am too bold in mentioning the fact that my own native country gave birth to Robert Burns. Much as we may regret the fact, it is not because we are a small nation, a small people, that no great writer of literature has yet appeared. I think he is coming. He will come some day, perhaps, under very humble circumstances and from a place where we never looked for him, not from learning, not from wealth; but from native ability and genius will come the great literature of Canada.
I have nothing to say against American magazines. I want to mention just this as I go along-it has nothing to do with the argument-as regards reading trashy stuff, perhaps the House will excuse my egotistical way of talking when I say I do not think I have read much trashy stuff for a number of years; but after being in this House and listening to speeches I felt an inclination to buy something trashy and perhaps spicy and read it, by way of change, as a setoff to the many speeches we have been listening to, my own included. I have nothing to say against American literature. I agree with the sentiments expressed by the member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). If we could get some British publications we should have the very best reading and we could delve into the deeps of the best literature and find something worth while. It may not be uninteresting for me to remark that this very day at lunch I was discussing with my desk mate (Mr. Hoey) certain articles in Hibbert's Journal, a magazine of the highest class. I mention this merely to let hon. members know that sometimes Progressives do read what is worth while.
Let me say a few words in regard to our national spirit. I remember well when I came to this country forty years ago that it struck me as rather strange to hear people coming into the province of Manitoba always speaking of particular provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, and so on. The words "Canada" and "Canadian" did not seem to be in use at all. I have noticed during recent years, however, and more so since the Great War, a striking growth in the Canadian national spirit; and, whatever may be said in the House sometimes in the course of debate,

Canadian Magazines
I believe that there is undoubtedly a Canadian national spirit among our people from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Whatever may be our differences, and although we may perhaps speak from a sectional point of view at times because our material interests lie in that direction, I do not think we are forgetting our birthright as Canadian citizens. All of us, I think, are willing to subscribe to a Canadian citizenship. I trust that in the years to come that feeling will grow and that our children will rise up with that pride in their nationality that they should feel.
I do not like introducing personal affairs into a debate, but as most hon. gentlemen know, I was not born a Canadian citizen. This fact notwithstanding, I am always proud to hear my children affirm their Canadian citizenship, although perhaps they are as ready to declare that their father is Scotch. I do not hear any one of them, however, say he is Scotch; they are Canadians all. So that one generation does the trick, so to speak, and there is no danger of any of our young people forgetting that they are Canadians.
I might say a word or two also in regard to our foreign population. I think sometimes we speak too disparagingly of those people who come from other countries and make their home in Canada. I had occasion while doing some public work in Winnipeg once to come into very close communication with a lady who superintended the children's hospital in the northern part of Winnipeg, and she said that the Canadian people in that city had a great deal to learn from the foreign population in the art of music and the entertainment that could be derived from that pleasurable source. The people who have a taste and a tafent for .music are well worth while and will in time make really good citizens.
Let me say once again that I have nothing to say against the United States. I believe that the future welfare of the world is to a very large extent bound up in the future of this North American continent. We find today in Europe trouble and distress, sorrow, hatred and envy everywhere. I do not suppose that the people over there are any better or any worse than we are. But we are placed in that position to-day that we can give a lead to the rest of the world, and I believe that this can be brought about by a perfect unity between the great nation to the south of us and our own Canadian people. I do not want it to be thought for a moment that I have anything but the most kindly feeling for the people of the United States. It seems to me that every effort should be made to develop that Canadian national spirit of which I have spoken. If the mover of the resolution-had been content to introduce it as it stands on the order paper I do not think I should have had any hesitation in supporting it. In regard to its bearing on the tariff I find that the Canadian Authors' Association makes this statement:
Canadian magazine and periodical publishers must pay duty on considerable equipment which they bring in from the United States and which is not made in Canada.
At least the mover of the amendment is willing that they should get that advantage by removing all restrictions on any materials they require for carrying on their business in Canada. I have no doubt that Canada can produce just as good magazines as are published in the United States, and I can realize, too, that they are working under very great difficulties. My sympathies are all with the publishers of Canadian magazines, and I only wish that something could be done to render their business profitable and enable them to produce magazines that would be read by the Canadian people. It has already been said that you cannot legislate people into reading good literature. I admit the truth of that dictum. Nearly everyone will pass through the stage of reading light and easily read literature until he acquires a taste for something better; and once having acquired that taste he will never go back to the trashy stuff. Once a man has got to know what is worth while in life and has learnt the secret of true living it is not likely that he will spend his time in the pursuit of what is unworthy. I have been wondering in these days when reading current literature why it is that we never get to-day the literature that is likely to last through the coming years. The best selling novels are read to-day, and to-morrow are forgotten and pass away. Why is it that today you find the novels of Sir Walter Scott and Charles Dickens still standing their ground and read by countless hundreds and thousands? There must be some reason. I do not know what the explanation is, but such is the fact. Everybody will agree that no matter how popular a novel may be to-day, in five years it will almost be forgotten. We are getting no literature that will live through the ages. It seems almost a bold thing to say, but it appears to me that the world has become so materialistic, and is looking so much to the almighty dollar, that we are not getting the literature that we should expect. It seems perhaps a little bold on my part to criticize literature, but I am stating honestly the view I have.
Reference has been made to the Montreal Witness, which I believe to be one of the most

Canadian Magazines

honest papers we have in the Dominion of Canada. I am not going to say anything about the Orange Sentinel. I get it all the time through the kindness of my hon. friend (Mr. Hocken), for I have a fair idea from whom it comes. I read it and enjoy it and I hope I am benefited by it. At the same time I might say a word in regard to the Witness. It has been in my household for the last thirty years and I am ready to make the statement that I have been greatly benefited thereby, because I know that, although I may not agree with what it says in all its editorials, it at least says what it .thinks and believes to be true. Now, I could support either the resolution or the amendment; it seems to me it does not make very much difference. But I think perhaps it is best to accept the amendment. The hon. member for Bonaventure took the wisest view when he suggested that the government use every endeavour to give Canadian publications all the advantage that could possibly be afforded and to encourage the reading of good Canadian literature.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to participate in this debate, but it seems to me one phase of the subject has not been touched on yet. Before I left the West I attended a meeting of business men who were consulting one another as to how they could reduce the cost of living, and, among other things discussed, they spoke of the cost of advertising. One Vancouver business firm stated that their advertising cost them as high as 7 per cent of their turnover. Another firm stated that they could not afford to reduce their advertising so long as American journals were circulating on the Canadian side and carrying so much advertising. The manager of this firm, which sold boots and shoes, said that the advertising in these American journals had a great effect on the Canadian people, inducing them to buy the goods thus advertised. Now, if there is anything Canada wants particularly at the present time it is a reduced cost of living, and if a tariff on these American magazines will reduce the cost of living in this country, then I say it is the duty of this government to impose such a duty as will keep them out.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The resolution of the hon. member
for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) is brief and quite simple. It expresses-shall I say-a pious hope, perhaps he will prefer if I say a patriotic hope, that we may all be able to encourage Canadian magazines and periodi-

cals. That is a sentiment which we can all subscribe to, and I want to vote for the resolution. But the moment we undertake to define the method by which this condition is to be brought about, we shall probably be divided in opinion, as the discussion has already shown. For the resolution itself I think we might all vote; I am sorry the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) has not given us a chance to vote for it as it stood on the Order Paper. True, it is very general, it may even be said to be very vague in its terms, but a resolution of this type, even though it be not specific, yet serves a good purpose in opening up such a general discussion as we have had this afternoon.
As I say, I am sorry the hon. member for Saskatoon has interposed his amendment. I regret to say that I am obliged to vote against it, and I hope the House will not adopt it. If free trade were part of our general tariff policy his amendment would be all right. But it is rather broad in its scope. He is going to place upon the free list quite a lot of things -paper, type, ink, presses, folders and a large list of goods now dutiable to a greater or less extent. Well now, the desire to relieve the press of some of its burdens is one that may appeal to our sympathies, but if you place those articles on the free list you may do very great injustice in other quarters. For example, take the item of paper. Without discussing whether or not paper should be protected, there is a duty on paper. If you strike that duty off you are putting the paper manufacturers of the country under an unexpected competition, and they will be able to say justly, " While you are having free trade in the thing we make, you are leaving us subject to duties on many of the things we use in our production." If you are going to strike out a very few items in the tariff which stand alone, it will be found in most cases that each item has some relation near or remote to some other item. Therefore if you make all the items covered by the amendment free, you are imposing a very unfair condition on the paper makers, the type makers and all the other manufacturers concerned.
I am sorry the amendment is made part of the resolution. The latter is based on a sentiment which I rather like, but I do not want to do any injustice even to the protected paper maker. I think the duties in the tariff to-day in relation to the press are not ungenerous, and I do not think the press has much reason to complain. At all events, while I would have pleasure in voting for the resolution of my hon. friend from West Tor-
