onto (Mr. Hocken) for, I repeat, it expresses an encouraging sentiment, I do not think the House ought to accept the amendment of my hon. friend from Saskatoon.
Right hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition): I was about to speak before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) rose in the hope that I might in some way influence his view. I have not very often been successful in that undertaking; probably I would not have been to-night.
I will ask the House to bear with me a very few minutes while I state with conciseness why I shall support the resolution in its original form and vote against the amendment. In the first place, let me say very frankly that I shall vote for the resolution in its original form, not because it is a mere expression of pious or patriotic hope. I shall vote for it because the mover (Mr.- Hocken) embodies in his resolution, and in the excellent speech he made in its support, specific, definite, understandable means by which the encouragement looked for in the resolution is to be given. I do not see much value in academic discussions urging the government to find some way of doing something good, unless we have something proposed by means of which that goal is to be reached.
The mover of the resolution has proposed one of two ways. He proposes a ten cents per pound duty on imported magazines, or a fifteen cents per pound duty on the advertising matter contained in such magazines. In my judgment one of those methods or a similar method is feasible. I do not wish to get off into the safety channel of the term "similar method" at all; I believe either of those methods is the right method and will bring the desired result, and I do not think that any other suggestion made in this debate will bring it about. I* venture to offer my reasons for that conclusion.
In the first place, I do not regard this as a question of encouraging good literature or bad literature, looked at from a moral standpoint. I do not say that that is not an important question. I believe it is. I do believe that the government has a duty in the way of discouraging, indeed banning, bad literature from a moral standpoint; but the way to do that is to ban it, and the government now has the power. That power has been exercised under previous governments; I have no reason to say that it is not being exercised under this government; but if it is not being exercised it ought to be exercised. If we admit the principle that all literature should be submitted to everybody for perusal, and simply let that policy take its effect, it
will carry us to lengths which, if described, no hon. member would be prepared to go.
The only extent to which the quality of the literature to be encouraged enters into this question is this: By a policy of encouraging Canadian literature by the means suggested would we be likely to get better literature from the moral standpoint; or from the Canadian standpoint? I think we would be likely to get better literature from both. I think it would be better from the moral standpoint for the simple reason that in a country like Canada of a sparse highly rural population, the general average of literature that will appeal to the people will probably be better than in a great cosmopolitan nation of the immensity of the United States. I think that may be concluded without assuming to ourselves any superior moral attributes. That we will get a more Canadian literature goes without question ,and therein is the principal subject that we have to discuss.
Then, the question comes: Is it better to have in this Dominion a thriving periodical monthly magazine industry, or is it not? Secondly, if it is, can it be done under present conditions? Can it be done without some of the means suggested by the mover of this resolution? Now I address myself to those questions.
I first of all want to affirm and press home to the government with all the emphasis in my power that this class of Canadian industry is as important as any other class of industry in this Dominion; that it is not only important that we do have a Canadian monthly periodical publication, but that it is so important that the necessity of any other single industry pales into insignificance compared to it. Now, why is it so important? Well, in the first place I believe the foundation as a propagator of opinions in a country to-day is the periodical literature. I believe that in the United States, in Great Britain, as well as in other countries, the editorial writer today does not occupy the same sphere of influence relatively that he did in years gone by; in the United States particularly and in England to a lesser degree his place has been taken by the magazine writer, by the contributor to the periodical literature of the countiy. There is disseminated in the most thorough and most forcible way, and in a manner that causes them to take root in the minds of people, principles of public policy, and public thinking, and these things take their flow from the writers in the periodical press rather than from the editorial writer as in days gone by I do not minimize the influence of editorial writing in the Canadian newspaper, but I do

Canadian Magazines

believe that the influence of the magazine writer has grown immensely in comparison. Very well; the magazine, then, the periodical paper, is of importance in any country. It is of especial importance in our own country, and I proceed to give the reasons why I think so.
We are peculiarly situated in this Dominion. We are as yet a small country. If we were a small country, though, as England was a small country in the days of Shakespeare, then the reasons that make it necessary for us to adopt special means would not be present; but we are not a small country in that sense at all. England in the time of Shakespeare was the' only English speaking country in the world. England had no competition, had no inflow of outside literature occupying the time and attention of her people. England had one language and one alone; the other countries around had their languages, consequently what market there was for the writings of Shakespeare, on the stage and in the printed paper, was virtually reserved for him and for his contemporaries.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question? He does not imagine that we have a Shakespeare in Canada today who is silent because of the great nation to the south?
What is the duty on magazines entering the United States? I ask for information.

I do not know, but for
the purposes of my argument we can assume it is nothing at all. Why would our magazines be bought in the United States? Our magazines catering to Canadian circulation naturally are concerned with subjects of peculiar interest to Canada. American magazines are concerned with subjects of peculiar interest to the United States. Consequently, American magazines for that reason would have a tremendous advantage over ours in their own country, and, of course, they carry American advertisements too. There is every reason in the world why they would have that advantage. The same case prevails here as prevails everywhere else. The Americans can attain to a tremendously larger area of business and, as a consequence, unless we are given some advantage in the Canadian market the American is in a position to swamp the Canadian market and keep out of business his Canadian competitor in the magazine business almost altogether. Why is it after all these years that we have so few Canadian magazines? It has simply been because the advantage of the American competitor has been such, year after year, that he has invaded the Canadian domain, got his advertising over here, his literature over here, and made his sales over here. He has invaded more and more as time went on, and now we have less and less Canadian periodical literature and more and more American periodical literature. Before I leave the duty question, let me say this. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) said that there was a duty on pulp coming from the United States, and, as I understood him that pulp had to go-first from Canadian mills to the United States, then be re-exported to this country, and that after being shipped to the United States it could be bought more cheaply than it could be bought from the Canadian manufacturer. What I say is this: If the Canadian manufacturer is discriminating against the Canadian consumer, there is a remedy in the hands of the government, and the government should not hesitate a day to put that remedy into effect. Of course, there are differences that could legitimately be taken into account, in the quantity purchased, for instance. If large purchases are made, probably a smaller purchase price might be justified; but for smaller purchases, if the American is given the advantage at all, the government has power under the law to take the duty off and the government ought to bring the Canadian manufacturer to terms by just that method. There
Canadian Magazines

i3 no excuse for discriminating against the Canadian consumer. I am not saying on my icsponsibility that that is being done. I can hardly believe that it is. I can hardly understand how it can be the fact. But it is the duty of the government to ascertain if it is the fact, and if there is discrimination, then the government should apply the remedy. Because there is abuse which it is in the power of the government to remedy under the law of the land, that is no reason why the principle itself should be removed.
Very well. Because of wholly dissimilar conditions there is no possibility of the Canadian magazine thriving as compared with the American magazine unless there is an advantage given in this country to the Canadian publisher. Why is it of extraordinary importance that this be done? It is for two reasons: First of all, magazine publishing is an industry the same as any other. It is entitled in my judgment to be treated the same as any other industry: it is entitled to the same advantage as any other industry in this country, the advantage in the home market over that enjoyed by its competitor in another country, for the sake of the men employed in the industry and in allied industries. In a word, in order that we may have it as an industry, it has the same claim as any other industry.
But that is not the major reason. There is a reason that appertains to this industry that has no relation to other industries at all. The magazine industry is one that contributes to the building up of Canadian spirit and Canadian national sentiment, and why should we apply our protective system to the manufacturer of cart wheels and screws and nails and Ford cars, and not apply it to the production of periodical literature in this country, is more than I can understand-and as I make that statement I make no particular attack or indictment against any government in particular. It seems to me that the reasons that apply to periodical monthly or weekly literature are powerful one hundredfold over those that apply to any other industry whatever.
I think the hon. member is perfectly logical in the position he takes. Why has not this protection been extended to this industry before?

I do not think I can give an adequate answer, but I will say this. I am not making this as an attack, as I stated before, on any party or any government. Under the late government the sale price of paper was entirely controlled until the courts declared that we had not power to exercise
fMr. Meighen.]
that control. That control existed for years, and I am pretty sure I am right in saying that under that control an advantage 10 p.m. was given to the Canadian consumer.
As a consequence, there would be an advantage there. Of that I speak with some diffidence, but if it will be helpful in any way to the hon. member I will be prepared for the sake of argument to admit that the late government should have given an advantage to Canadian periodical publications and did not. I am inclined to think though that through the greater period of its existence it did. I was emphasizing the importance of giving something in the way of fair treatment at least, and you must give the advantage in the Canadian market if you are going to give fair treatment to Canadian periodical literature. What is going to be the result-yes, what to-day is the result of the consumption of American publications in this country in the degree that they are being consumed now? Why, by the character of the literature of the country, by the spirit that animates that literature the whole mind of the nation is nourished and supported. What is going to be the consequence if the child in Canada reads the publications of Atlanta, Georgia, reads the publications of New York, reads all these literary productions that are inspired by American spirit and American sentiment, and makes that the mental nourishment of his life? If that is all right, if that is necessary on this alleged free trade or free literature principle, it would necessarily be right that they should also have free access to our schools. Why not let them also on the same principle provide the literature for the children of our schools, make our readers, sell them on a commercial basis? That is aD extreme illustration.
Hear, hear.

But only by that can
one make oneself clear to some hon. gentlemen. In a word, if government is to exercise no control whatever over literature, it follows that we must let the American publisher right into the schoolroom and let him there feed the mind of the young on just as free a basis as would the Canadian writer and publisher.
Now what I want to urge upon the government is this: we should make certain that the young writer of this country, whose thoughts are Canadian and British, gets an avenue for his energies and a reward for his efforts in this Canada of ours. We have too many of them across the line. I can name them on the fingers of my hand now. I know men who went through college with me who

Canadian Magazines
to-day are eminent in literary work, and I do not think I know one who is not a citizen of the United States. These men get access to these widely circulating American publications that can pay far more than any little struggling magazine in this country can pay. Put the Canadian magazine in a position where it will get the same circulation	as that now enjoyed in Canada
by the American magazine, give it the body of that circulation, and then it will be able to offer inducements to the young aspiring Canadian writer; there will be something to keep him in his own Dominion and the mind of the Canadian people will be fed on literature produced in Canada and animated by the spirit and aspirations of this country. Surely that is of vital importance to us.
There is one thing I know that will meet with the approval of hon. members to my left. On this question of the British preference I am ready to go the whole extent of their 50 per cent,-yes, I will double that preference. I am willing to make the preference to British magazines 100 per cent, and I will tell hon. members why. This is a British country, and I cannot speak in too high terms of the excellent speech in support of the resolution made by the hon. member for Bon-aventure (Mr. Marcil) and of the good British sentiments that he expressed. He made as sound an argument for protection, without mentioning the word " protection " of course as I have ever heard in this House. There is no reason at all why we need protect Canadian literature against British literature. The more British literature circulates here the better. It will never circulate to the serious detriment of Canadian publications. It has too far to come and is too old when it reaches us. The difficulty will be, and is to-day, that we do not get enough of good British magazine literature in this Dominion, and Britain has excellent literature of this character in her publications. The difficulty is we do not get enough of it. We should have no prohibition or discouragement whatever of that literature, and should not interfere with the access of that character of literature to Canada. The prohibition of the Atlantic itself is quite sufficient, because literature, even periodical monthly literature, that is a few weeks old is usually too old for very wide consumption. However, having regard to the necessity for the spread of British thought and British spirit through this country, we are not going to get too much of it, though we put no ban on it, though we place no duty on it and though we have no obstacle at all in the way of it reaching Canada.
What we need to do is to give the Canadian competitor here a chance against the man who really to-day is destroying his business and preventing its success for years, and who is stifling the production of Canadian literature, and we need to do that now. How can that be done? I think I have shown it cannot be done by the method suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans). That would lead us to extremes to which we cannot go, and if we went to those extremes we would be just where we commenced, and we would not have achieved any of the objects whatsoever. It is all right to pass a fine resolution about encouraging literature, but let us be practical. How are you going to encourage it? Those engaged in the business have devised this plan. They say "Put a duty of 15 per cent upon the advertising contained in the magazines, or 15 cents a pound or 10 cents a pound upon the magazines themselves". Of the two I am disposed to favour the first, for this reason, advertising matter is now taxed, provided only that it does not come within the folds of the magazine. If it comes by itself, it is taxed, but if you put some spicy story with it and call it a magazine, it is not taxed at all. That does not appear to me to be reasonable. It seems to me it should be taxed in whatever form it comes, and by taxing the advertising matter you also do away with some of the advantage that the American advertiser has as against the Canadian advertiser- an advantage very well determined by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). In other words, you achieve two very important objects by a duty in that form. You do not achieve either of those objects so directly by a duty upon the magazine itself. Therefore, I am disposed to favour the proposition that we place a reasonably fair duty on the advertising matter contained in American periodical literature, that we do it without delay, and that we seek to attain the goal by this method, and if this method fail, then if we consider the goal high enough and desirable enough to attain we will resort to other methods to reach it.

I did not intend to take part in this very interesting debate, but the speech of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) to which we have all listened with very great interest, has led me to make a few observations, perhaps, in a sense somewhat opposed to those which he has addressed to the House. Apparently the literature of this country has to be encouraged by a protective tariff. Has not the result to the industrial life of this country of a protective tariff taught the

Canadian Magazines

right hon. leader of the Opposition how futile that method is? We have had in this country, for the last 50 years or thereabouts, a protective tariff, and in most lines of industry or manufacture, the protected manufacturers ask, not for less protection but more protection, and I take it if literature is to be protected by a tariff of 10 or 20 per cent, in a few years the authors and journalists will come before the House and say "Our genius does not afford us a livelihood, and unless we have the protection of a 40 or 50 per cent tax on literature we will have to go out of business".
I was somewhat pleased and interested in hearing the historical allusion of the right hon. leader of the Opposition. Shakespeare was one who wrote for a comparatively small audience. The people who lived close by spoke different languages, and that is where his success lies. Might I point out to my right hon. friend that if ever there was a man who borrowed from contemporary literature in his day, or from literature which shortly before had been prevalent in other countries, it was the same divine William Shakespeare. Take his plays Romeo and Juliet, the Two Gentlemen of Verona. Did he not get his plots from Italy? When he wrote his immortal Hamlet, was it not from Denmark that he drew the theme of his drama? I would recommend my hon. friend to turn from Shakespeare to the other great contemporary, or almost contemporary, John Milton, and there he will learn that literature, that the intelligence of a nation and that the creation of a human soul are not propagated or helped by the commercial 10 per cent or 20 per cent, but that if there is anything under which genius flourishes it is liberty and the air of freedom, and not a protective tariff or adventitious aids of that sort.
How is a nation developed? My hon. friend is anxious to have a Canadian spirit in this country. I am anxious too, but perhaps we would proceed by different methods in endeavouring to arrive at the desired result. I do say that we could arouse a Canadian spirit in this country first of all by teaching the boys and the girls and the men and the women of Canada that we should be Canadians first and all the time; that this country is the country to which we owe our first allegiance and that there is in the world no other country which has a greater claim over us than this country in which we live; in which our children have been bom and in which we hope to lay our bones when we pass to the other side.
jMr. McMaster.]
May I point out to the leader of the Opposition and to all those who agree with him, that to expect to keep out American magazine literature in this country by a 10 per cent or a 15 per cent tariff on advertising matter is just about as likely to succeed as Mrs. Partington when she tried to keep away the waves that were coming on the advancing tide. The leader of the Opposition, if he really believes in his theory, is the modern King Canute who sat by the seaside and told the waves not to advance any further. This magazine business is not on a commercial basis at all. It is the advertising that pays for those magazines.
Is that not commercial?
That is literature.

No, it is not iiterature. We have been talking about literature so much that it might be as well if we had a definition of literature. There are books for the moment and books for all time, and books for all time compose literature and the other things are not literature. What makes the American magazine circulate so much in Canada is the fact that the Canadian people like to read the stories which are in those magazines and one reason why the stories are good is because there is a great deal of advertising in those magazines and the publishers are able to pay very large sums of money for those stories and to command the best writers. I do not think, whether we like to do this or not, any ten or fifteen per cent tariff will affect that situation. If Canada is to have a great magazine literature and if Canadian literary genius is to be developed, it is not going to be developed in that way. Of that I am quite positive. But there is one suggestion I have as to the development of a Canadian national spirit and as to the growth of Canadian periodical literature. It is this, that our papers should not appeal only to one class or one section or one province in the country. How splendid it would be, for instance, if that journal, conducted by a distinguished member of this House, printed one page in French! How it might add to its circulation in provinces other than Ontario and what a help it might be to the development of a true Canadian patriotic sentiment that would cut right across the division of races and provinces and even all ecclesiastical differences, I will not call that religion!
What about this amendment? I am extremely sympathetic with the idea of the amendment; but I am afraid that when we go to reform the tariff, we shall not be able to reform it fairly or reasonably by picking

Canadian Magazines
85a
out just a few things of this sort in a discussion of this kind. The tariff will have to be amended; I believe the imperative interests of this country demand that it should be reduced; but it should be reduced, it seems to me only after a careful examination of the whole field, and I am inclined to the opinion that although I am deeply sympathetic with this amendment, it is not the proper way to go about this business.
Let me say just this to those who, after seeing shoes taxed and stockings taxed and clothes taxed and hats taxed, now propose to tax even the magazine which we take to while away a pleasant hour-you may make a logical argument from the protectionist point of view for taxing the people of Canada in order to encourage the native production of magazines, but there is one thing which should remain untaxed and that is the free flow of ideas into a country. That is something that we should not tax even if we are protectionists. May I say this, that any industry that cannot stand on its own feet in a country is commercially not an asset, but a liability to that country, because the producers of a country who are carrying the burden, have to carry just so much larger a burden. The danger in Canada-and it is a very real danger, is though the friends sitting in the left hand corner of the chamber, do not seem to realize it-that if you impose this burden of maintaining a non-economic industry and that burden of encouraging and producing and forcing into economic life another non-economic industry, you may make the burden too heavy for the industries which are really economic. That is a real danger to this country. There was a cartoon which someone told me about the other day. The German goose was being held by a French soldier and the French soldier was pressing its neck and saying: "Lay, confound you, lay." But that is the position in which the natural producers of this country are more and more getting into with the burden which the non-economic industries of this country are placing upon them. They are getting into a position of saying: "We won't lay."

It would be
very interesting if the hon. gentleman would tell us, why he says: "more and more " every day.

I would say that "Every day, in every way, our protectionists are getting greedier and greedier." We have had an interesting speech from the leader of the Opposition. Every journalist, every magazine writer, who hopes for better things under a
protectionist tariff, every magazine proprietor who sees great profits flowing in when 10 per cent is put on his competitor from the United States will no doubt echo and spread over the Dominion what the right hon. gentleman has said. But after all, it is founded upon a fallacy and when I hear-because I was not in this House years ago-the echoes of the speeches, those strong low tariff speeches, that the leader of the Opposition made for lower taxes on implements of production coming into this country, I have a sort of sneaking feeling that in his heart he agrees more with me than he does with himself.

Mr. Speaker, just a few words before we vote.
I think the remarks that were made by the leader of the Agrarian party (Mr. Forke) as to the dullness of speeches in this House have had the effect of brightening up this particular debate. Certainly, since he spoke, there has been a little more pep in it than there was in the earlier part of the day.
Let me express my grafification at, and deep appreciation of, the temper of the speech delivered by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). He is an old newspaper man; he knows a good deal about the publishing business, something about which I think the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) is about as ignorant as he is of trade questions. The hon. member for Bonaventure was speaking out of experience and of course he was speaking wisely, and I am sure his contribution to the debate has been very valuable. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) tries to be facetious at my expense. Well, Sir, I do not think that need bother anyone; it certainly does not perturb me. Any man who stands up in this House and tries to discount the genius of William Shakespeare cannot, I think, be taken seriously by anyone. It is pretty late in the day to charge Shakespeare with plagiarism or anything of that kind. I am not asking for the removal" of duties; that removal would not provide the remedy required in this case. I cited the fact that the publishers have to pay duty on raw materials; but I pointed out to the House the injustice under which they labour in having no protection themselves. None of them, as far as I know, asked for the removal of the duties on paper, ink, or anything else. But, Sir, they think that they ought to have protection from the competition, which is unfair, from the other side of the line. The American publication that comes here is dumped on this market and it seems to me it should come under the dumping
Canadian Magazines

clause of the tariff as clearly as any other manufactured goods that might be brought here. American magazines are sold in this country at less than the price of the paper and press work would amount to if they were printed here; and how it is expected that Canadian publishers can compete with that is beyond my comprehension.
I do not wish to go over anything that has been already said, but we have got to this point: the free importation of American periodicals means the forced exportation of the brains of authors and the talents of artists of this country. That is what it amounts to. Any man who makes a mark as a writer here does not stay here to serve a Canadian magazine. We cannot expect him to. Can we expect a man who has talent to write an article for which he can get $1,000 in the United States and sell it here for $100 or $200? And the same thing applies to artists as well as to writers. Any person in the magazine industry, whether a writer, an artist, an engraver or a business man, as soon as he demonstrates his capacity in his particular line, is taken over the border by reason of the enormous circulations and revenues which the American publications enjoy. It is only about a year and a half ago that the man who was editing the most largely circulated paper in this country was taken off that paper, by a salary tWice as large to go to Philadelphia. I am speaking not of a writer particularly, but an editor; and there is a marked distinction. And that applies to every man on a Canadian magazine. Just in proportion to the ability that Canadians display is the speed with which [DOT] they go over the line and assist in producing magazines that come into this country and make it impossible for Canadian publishers to compete. If there is any industry in this country that should be protected it is the one that will teach the people to be Canadians and will try to interpret one province to another, using the talents of Canadians to develop Canadian ideals and a Canadian sentiment from one end of the country to the other.
Amendment negatived.
Main motion agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to suggest to the hon. gentleman who has moved this resolution that it is a very important departure from old parliamentary practice, and I do not think it should be adopted hurriedly. The matter might at a later day be referred to the committee on rules and be considered in connection with other rules, but I would ask my hon. friend not to press his resolution to-night. This is an old established practice of parliament, and although there may be reasons for a change, I do not think the practice should be changed without much more deliberation than we are able to give it to-night.
